docs.title: Horses
docs.summary: Buy a horse at a Stable, use its speed and gallop carefully, and keep it fed when you travel together.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A Stable offers three horses for the town's game day; their stats and prices vary.
> - Speed affects riding pace, while Stamina affects how long a horse can gallop.
> - Galloping spends the horse's breath. It becomes winded at zero and must recover before galloping again.
> - Oats feed a horse for 24 hours; apples last four hours and build more bond.

## Choose a horse

Visit a Stable to compare the horses offered that day. Each has four stats: Speed, Stamina, Endurance and Strength. Speed changes the riding pace; Stamina sets the gallop reserve; Endurance affects breath use and recovery; Strength matters when the horse pulls a team. The horse's starting stats influence its price, so compare the profile with how you expect to travel.

## Ride and gallop

Riding is faster than walking, but galloping uses breath. When the reserve runs out, the horse is winded and cannot gallop until at least 30% of its breath has returned. A starving horse cannot gallop. Entering a building or dungeon dismounts you; you do not automatically remount when you leave.

## Feed and care

You can feed a horse oats or an apple. Oats last 24 hours; an apple lasts four hours and is a stronger treat for bond. Online, the Horse care setting is yours to choose, and its default is Boons (which rules apply online). In Boons, hunger does not reduce the horse's stats. Under Hard care, hunger lowers stats and a loaded wagon can slow a team according to its horses' Strength. In any care tier, a starving horse cannot gallop. A horse at a Stable is fed there; a horse waiting in the world grazes enough not to starve.

Your own Horse Cart and Cargo setting governs whether its mod places horses and wagons in the world online. Stable purchases and the port's riding rules are separate from that placement feature (wagons and hauling). For the route itself, see overworld travel; when you want to meet a companion on the road, see party travel.

## Common mistakes

- Galloping a horse that is already winded. It cannot gallop until at least 30% of its breath returns, and a starving horse never can. Cost: you walk the last stretch or fail to outrun an ambush.
- Leaving the horse unfed before a long ride. Oats last 24 hours and an apple four; a starving horse cannot gallop, and under Hard care hunger lowers its stats (which rules apply online). Cost: a slower journey.
- Buying a horse for a one-off inter-city trip. A hired carriage charges a small daily fare and needs no feed, while a horse costs its Stable price and must be fed. Cost: gold spent on a mount you did not need.

## Next

- Ships and passage
- Portal Stones

docs.title: Ships and passage
docs.summary: Book passage aboard a friendly ship at a port, follow its sailed route, and stay aboard until the voyage ends.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - At a port, activate a friendly ship and ask its master where the vessel will sail.
> - Passage is available on a Large Boat, Small Ship or Carrack, not a Rowboat or Large Galley.
> - The destination must be a known port beyond the local landfall range.
> - The fare follows the map distance, and you pay it even if you own a ship. Hulls cost from 4,000 to 200,000 gold.
> - Passage is a sailed journey. Stay aboard; stepping off ends the passage.

## Book passage

Find a friendly vessel moored at a port berth and activate it. If the hull carries passengers, its master offers the ports you know that are beyond the berth's immediate landfall range. The offer is ordered by distance. You cannot book a destination you have not discovered.

Only a Large Boat, Small Ship or Carrack carries a passenger. A Rowboat is too small, and a Large Galley does not moor for passage. The game quotes the fare before you accept. Its price is based on the voyage's map distance and is charged even if you own a ship.

## During the voyage

The ship sails the route; it does not teleport you. Stay aboard until the journey ends. If you step ashore, go over the side or enter another place, the passage ends and your goods come ashore with you. If a fight interrupts the voyage while you remain aboard, the captain resumes sailing after a pause.

Passage serves travel within the Bay. Ships beyond the Veil sail the Eltheric Ocean and cannot carry you back to Bay ports by this service. Owning and outfitting a ship opens later; see The Harbormaster's Word.

## Fares and prices

A port passage's fare is 25 gold plus 25 more for each full 24 map pixels of the voyage's longest map distance. Short hops are cheap; a long crossing climbs in 25-gold steps. The fare is the same whether or not you already own a ship.

Hulls are sold at a port's Shipyard, cheapest first:

| Hull | Price | Sold as |
|---|---:|---|
| Rowboat | 4,000 gold | Parts for your pack; launch it at any water |
| Large Boat | 8,000 gold | A deed in your Fleet |
| Small Ship | 100,000 gold | A deed in your Fleet |
| Carrack | 150,000 gold | A deed in your Fleet |
| Large Galley | 200,000 gold | A deed in your Fleet |

The shipyard also buys hulls back and handles refits, and its Crew Hall hires named hands. See Owning a ship for the Fleet, the hold and upkeep.

Travelling on the map under Immersive Travel, which is on for shared rooms online, adds its own daily rates. A carriage trip pays 1 gold for each whole day on land plus one more day's fee. A ship trip adds 15 gold for each sea day when you do not own the ship, plus 10 gold for each sea day for the captain and crew, which you pay even when the ship is yours. Sea days are counted as full 24 map pixels plus one.

> [!online] Online rule
> The port passage and its fare are the port's own service. The daily carriage and ship rates above belong to Immersive Travel, whose fare rules the room forces at their shipped values online. Only the map's cosmetic dots and roads stay your own setting.

## Common mistakes

- Expecting passage to be free because you own a ship. The port fare is charged regardless; only the map's 15-gold daily rental disappears.
- Trying to book a landlocked destination. Passage reaches ports; inland places need another route.
- Ignoring the daily rates. A ship trip on the map is not one flat fare; the captain's 10 gold is charged for every sea day.
- Confusing a crowded quay with a berth. Activate a moored ship, not the dock around it.

## Next

- Portal Stones
- Mages Guild teleport

docs.title: Portal Stones
docs.summary: Spend Welkynd Shards on a Portal Stone, choose a destination under the open sky, and let nearby travelers step through.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Any shop can sell a Portal Stone for 5 Welkynd Shards.
> - Use the stone under open sky at a valid place to choose a destination; confirming consumes one stone and opens a portal for 30 seconds.
> - Other nearby players can use the open portal too.
> - A portal cannot bypass danger, a duel, siege wards or a journey already under way.

## Buy and use a stone

Buy a Portal Stone from a shop counter with Welkynd Shards. The stone is always available at the counter; it is not a shelf item bought with gold. Use it from your pack or hotbar, choose a place on the map, then confirm. Closing the map without choosing does not spend the stone.

The portal appears in front of you and remains open for 30 seconds. Walk through it to arrive at the chosen place. Online, nearby players can also pass through it while it stands.

## Limits

You need open sky and room to place the portal. You cannot open one indoors, in water, aboard a boat or on a standalone street. The portal is held while you are dead or moving, in a duel, under siege wards, near enemies or already travelling. Online teleport boundaries also apply: a Portal Stone cannot cross into or out of the Open Zone or cross the Veil.

> [!warning] Save the stone for a clear moment
> Enemies nearby or a journey in progress prevent portal use. The stone does not provide an escape from those rules.

## Common mistakes

- Saving the stone for an escape from a fight. The portal is held near enemies, so a Portal Stone cannot pull you out of a losing fight (the map and danger). Cost: you die with the stone still in your pack.
- Trying to open one indoors or on a street. The stone needs open sky and room to place the portal, so a refused attempt wastes the moment you needed it.
- Expecting a Portal Stone to cross the Open Zone or the Veil. Online boundaries apply to it just as they do to the Mages Guild teleport. Cost: a journey planned around a teleport that cannot be made.

## Next

- Mages Guild teleport
- Party travel

buy-and-use-a-stone.title: Buy and use a stone
buy-and-use-a-stone.excerpt: Buy a Portal Stone from a shop counter with Welkynd Shards. The stone is always available at the counter; it is not a shelf item bought with gold. Use it from your pack or hotbar, choose a place on the map, then confirm. Closing the map without choosing does not spend the stone.

limits.title: Limits
limits.excerpt: You need open sky and room to place the portal. You cannot open one indoors, in water, aboard a boat or on a standalone street. The portal is held while you are dead or moving, in a duel, under siege wards, near enemies or already travelling. Online teleport boundaries also apply: a Portal Stone cannot cross into or out of the Open Zone or cross the Veil.

docs.title: Mages Guild teleport
docs.summary: Use the Mages Guild's rank-gated teleport service from a guild hall, and keep Recall's separate anchor rules in mind.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Any Mages Guild member can teleport from a guild hall by turning on paid teleportation in their own Travel
>   Options settings: (8 − rank) × 200 gold a trip.
> - The free service is for rank 8 and above, which online means a chapter's officers and Master.
> - Recall is a spell that uses a one-use anchor. It is separate from the guild service.
> - Online, these teleports cannot cross into or out of the Open Zone or cross the Veil.

## Guild service

Use the service at a Mages Guild hall and choose a destination from its teleport map. There are two ways in:

| Route | Who | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Free service | Members at rank 8 or above | Free |
| Paid service | Any member, once you turn on Enable Paid Teleportation in your Travel Options settings (off by default) | (8 − your rank) × 200 gold per teleport: 1,400 gold at rank 1, 200 at rank 7 |

> [!online] Online rule: rank 8 is a chapter seat
> Online, your own guild rank stops at 7. Ranks 8 and 9 are chapter seats: each Mages Guild chapter has three
> officers (rank 8) and one Master (rank 9). So the free service is for chapter officers. For everyone else, the paid
> service is the way to use guild teleport, and its switch is your own: Travel Options' paid-teleport setting is not
> one of the travel switches DFO forces online (which rules apply online).

You do not need to cast a spell to use the guild service. It is a Mages Guild service, not the Mysticism spell Recall. The guild ranks themselves are covered with the NPC guilds.

## Recall

Recall is the Mysticism Teleport effect. Cast it once to set an anchor and again to return to that place. The anchor records the position and context, including whether it was set outside, inside a building or in a dungeon; using it consumes the anchor. You can set an anchor inside and cast Recall from an interior.

Online refusal rules prevent Recall from entering or leaving the Open Zone and from crossing the Veil. These same world boundaries apply to the guild teleport service.

## Common mistakes

- Waiting for rank 8 before using the teleport. Any member can use the paid service once Enable Paid Teleportation is on; waiting for a chapter seat costs travel time (NPC guilds). Cost: days of carriage fares.
- Forgetting to turn the setting on. Paid teleportation is off by default; a member who stands at the hall expecting a port finds nothing and takes a carriage instead. Cost: a fare and a session detour.
- Planning a Recall that crosses a boundary. Recall and the guild service both refuse the Open Zone and the Veil, so such a trip has to be walked or sailed (Portal Stones). Cost: a plan that cannot be executed.

## Next

- Party travel
- The map and danger

docs.title: Party travel
docs.summary: Meet a party leader through an offered fast trip, confirm the fare, and arrive beside them without advancing world time.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Use /leader to offer to travel to your party leader; use /travel to answer the leader's round.
> - Each follower accepts their own fare before travelling.
> - Party travel arrives at the world's present and does not advance world time.
> - It cannot cross the Open Zone boundary or the Veil.

## Travel to a leader

When you are in a party (meeting other players) and your leader is on another map pixel, /leader offers you a fast trip to them. Accept the offer and you arrive near the leader, or at the place's door if the leader is inside. The prompt shows your fare before you confirm; each travelling member pays their own.

The leader can gather the party for a round of travel with /travel. Followers have 30 seconds to join after the party sets out. If you miss that window, the offer points you back to /leader instead.

## Boundaries

Party travel is a fast trip to the leader, not a walked Overworld route. It arrives at the world's present and does not spend journey time. Online boundaries still apply: party travel cannot cross into or out of the Open Zone or across the Veil. Use the Overworld Travel View for a walked route.

## Common mistakes

- Missing the 30-second follow window. After the party sets out, a late follower loses the offer and must fall back to /leader and pay their own fare again. Cost: fares and time.
- Assuming the leader's fare covers yours. Each travelling member pays their own fare; a follower who cannot pay is left behind. Cost: a split party.
- Trying to cross the Open Zone or the Veil with party travel. The fast trip is refused at both boundaries (Open Zone, Eltheric Ocean). Cost: a wasted attempt and lost group time.

## Next

- The map and danger
- Overworld travel

docs.title: Your first week
docs.summary: A session plan for levels 1 to 5, the introduction questlines they open, and what to check before you spend.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Register before you invest in professions, trade, guilds or event rewards; a guest's work in those systems is not recorded.
> - Bank your carried gold before you leave town: an ordinary death takes one tenth of it.
> - The Court Crafter and A Seat at the Table open at level 2, Written in the Stars and The Merchant's Road at level 3, The Smith's Secrets at level 4 and The Harbormaster's Word at level 5.
> - Letters reach you only outdoors in a town by day, and a new line starts no sooner than an hour of character time after the last.
> - Star refunds are free below Renown 10; the two-craft limit above Journeyman is permanent.

## The first five levels

Levels 1 to 5 are where DFO Online hands out its first systems. Each introduction questline opens at a set character level, arrives as a courier letter, and sends you to one NPC in your current town. Two habits carry the stretch: keep your purse in the bank, and register before you invest in anything the account service tracks.

## Before you invest an evening

Register early. A guest can play at once, but professions and Stores, the global market, player guilds, Marks, Soul Cakes and Starfall claims are refused or not recorded. Registration adds a username and password to the same account and keeps what you have done; save the eight recovery codes. See Your account.

Bank before you leave. An ordinary online death returns you to a safe point at half health and takes one tenth of the gold you carry, rounded down. Banked gold and letters of credit are outside that penalty, and any bank counter reaches the same Empire account online. See Dying online and Banks.

Join a guild for private work. NPC guilds take applications at their halls; the check is standing and guild skills, not a joining fee. The design records point a new character at the Fighters Guild hall in Gothway Garden. Guild quests give you your own dungeon and a reward card, and guild training stops at skill 50. See The NPC guilds.

## A session plan

1. Leave Privateer's Hold for Gothway Garden.
2. Register, bank your gold and join a guild at its hall.
3. Take one guild quest or a notice-board bounty and finish it; a quest dungeon is your own instance.
4. Sell the spare loot, keep what you can use, and bank the purse again.
5. Stand outdoors in town by day until a letter arrives; the Quests tab shows what each line waits for.
6. Do the step the letter opened. The next step of that line waits an hour of character time, and no new line begins while another line's first letter is on its way.

## The introductions, level by level

| Level | Questline | Where the letter sends you | What it starts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | The Court Crafter (registered account) | A court crafter at the local general store | Gathering, crafting, Professions and Stores |
| 2 | A Seat at the Table | A tavern regular at a tavern | The card tables; its second step waits for The King's Gambit |
| 3 | Written in the Stars (online) | An astrologer at a temple | The Firmament and its stars |
| 3 | The Merchant's Road | A stable master's note; collect the load at a tavern | Wagons and hauling |
| 4 | The Smith's Secrets | An armorer at an armory | Sockets and the Reforge; its steps wait for Loot rarity |
| 5 | The Harbormaster's Word | A harbormaster at a tavern | Ships and the sea; its steps wait for Naval Combat |

The steps pay gold as well as teach: the level 2–4 lines pay 100–200 gold a step, and the level 5 sea line 200–400 (the quest scripts' ranges). A step starts wherever you are, so be in a proper town: the Court Crafter needs a general store, and the others a tavern, armory or temple. A step that cannot begin says so and waits a day of character time.

## Before you spend

| Choice | What it costs | What to know first |
|---|---|---|
| Firmament star | One point per star; Renown supplies two per level after the first, and the first sign is free | A refund is free below Renown 10; after that it costs 10 Marks a star, and a whole-sky respec costs 10000 gold |
| Craft rank | 10 × rank² XP a track: rank 50 is 25,000 and Master is 100,000 | Only two crafts may pass Journeyman (rank 50); the account service holds a third at rank 50 |
| Mastery | One of five slots, spent when a skill reaches 100 | A mastery can never be undone: two primary, two major and one minor slot |
| Gold | One tenth of the carried purse per death; the large purchases are later | Bank it. A skill swap costs 100,000 gold and a path reset 200,000 |

## Common mistakes

- Playing for days as a guest. The profession work, market trades and event rewards you earned were not recorded and cannot be claimed after you register.
- Carrying the purse into a dungeon. One death takes a tenth of everything you carry.
- Pushing a third craft to 50. It is held one experience point short of rank 51 for good; the two crafts you raise above 50 are the permanent pair.
- Waiting for letters in the wilds or at night. The courier needs you outdoors in a town by day.
- Refunding stars after Renown 10 without counting the cascade. A connecting star takes its dependents with it, and each is charged.

## Next

- Levelling online
- Renown

- Planning a session
- The progression map

docs.title: Levelling online
docs.summary: How skills, levels, attribute points and the health floor work online.
headings: How a skill becomes a level
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Use your class skills: primary and major skills, plus your strongest minor, drive character levels.
> - Skill uses build toward a raise; they do not raise a skill with every action.
> - Each online level gives you 5 attribute points to allocate.
> - Your maximum Health cannot fall below the online class-and-Endurance floor.

## How a skill becomes a level

The game tallies eligible skill use and periodically checks whether a skill can rise. The check runs after more than 360
minutes (six game hours) of game time. The number of uses needed depends on the skill, its current value, your class's advancement
multiplier, and your character level. Stronger custom classes need more uses; higher skills and character levels also
raise the cost. The Growth panel shows your skill and level progress.

Character level follows a weighted skill sum: all primary skills, all major skills except the lowest, and the highest
minor skill count. Every 15 points of eligible progress advances the calculated level. When a level is owed, open the
level-up screen to apply it; each visit applies one level.

> [!online] Online attribute points
> Online gives a fixed pool of 5 attribute points at every level. Offline Daggerfall Unity rolls 4–6. You choose where
> the online points go, so Endurance can affect both future health gains and the health floor described below.

## The health floor

Your online maximum Health is kept at or above the value your class would have at your current level using average
health rolls and your current permanent Endurance. A low roll can still affect the health added at a level, but it
cannot leave your maximum below that floor. Raising Endurance can lift the floor retroactively.

This is an online layer; it does not rewrite your saved offline health rolls. For the other effects of attributes and
the actions that train individual skills, see Attributes and skills.

## Common mistakes

- Expecting every use to raise a skill. Uses accumulate until the skill's check is ready; the ticker is not a
  per-action progress bar.
- Treating character level and Renown as one ladder. Character level comes from skill progress. Renown
  is a separate online track.

## Next

- Renown
- The Firmament

- The progression map

docs.title: Planning a session
docs.summary: Turn one hour or one evening into a route through caps, event windows, questline letters and travel.
headings: Know which clock you are racing
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Decide the session's one goal before leaving town: a capped daily, an event window, a questline step or a dungeon.
> - Renown is capped at 15000 XP per account per clock hour; combat Marks at 150 a UTC day; court writs at 3; the bank exchange at 300 Marks.
> - Questline letters arrive outdoors in a town by day, and a new line starts no more than once per character hour.
> - Travel is real time: a carriage costs about 1 gold a travel day, a Portal Stone 5 shards, and the trip back counts.

## Choose the session's goal

A session works when it chases one thing. Three kinds cover most evenings:

- A cap run collects the day's bounded rewards while they are available: combat Marks, a court writ, the bank exchange, the day's gathering nodes.
- An event run puts you at a world event inside its window: a Dagon's Breach, a town raid, the sea serpent, a Motherlode, a Starfall night.
- A progress run advances something uncapped: a questline step, a dungeon, a profession rank or a skill.

Mix them only in order: take the capped reward first, because it is the part a longer session cannot recover, then spend the rest of the time on progress. Catching up in short sessions has the same advice in short form.

## Know which clock you are racing

DFO uses several clocks, and a "daily" rule does not mean local midnight.

| Clock | What runs on it | What it means for a session |
|---|---|---|
| Shared game day | The event clock. One game day is 1,440 classic minutes, and the shared clock runs 12 classic minutes per real minute, so a game day is two real hours. | Event windows can open and close inside one sitting. |
| UTC day | Combat Marks (150), bank exchange (300 Marks), court writs (3), Motherlodes (three), Starfall claims (nine), gathering node slots. | The reset can happen mid-session, at a UTC boundary, not at your local midnight. |
| Clock hour | Renown (15000 XP), profession requests, Marks operations, market posts. | These reset at the top of each real hour; they are rate limits, not daily allowances. |
| World timers | Dungeon respawns (20 minutes ordinary, 40 elite); gate, raid and serpent phases. | These belong to the world, not to your account; waiting does not "earn" anything. |

The full tables are in Caps, timers and resets and World events and their clock.

The event clock's practical windows:

- Dagon's Breach rises once a game day (every two real hours); its open phase runs 20:00–22:00 on the game clock, about ten real minutes. Its omen starts at 17:00 game time.
- Town raids use a two-game-hour window, about ten real minutes, and the start varies within the game day.
- The sea serpent rises on every second game day — every four real hours — with its phases on that day's clock.
- Motherlodes are three scheduled lodes per UTC day, each with a two-hour open window and a warning before it opens; the source does not publish one fixed hour for each, so use the live warning.
- Starfall runs during the seasonal Witches' Festival with its own falling-star windows and a daily claim limit.

## A one-hour plan

1. Start in a town. Bank the purse, repair, sell spare loot, and check the event display before you commit to a direction.
2. Read the Quests tab. A step that is due now is worth more than a random dungeon; a letter you cannot receive away from town can wait.
3. Pick one destination and add the return trip. A fight that takes fifteen minutes but forty to reach is a ninety-minute session, not a one-hour one.
4. Take the capped reward first. If a gate or raid is close, fit it in before the dungeon; if the Marks ceiling is already spent, skip combat about Marks and do the progress activity.
5. Leave a buffer. Bank, repair and reach a safe town before you log out; dying with the session's takings carried is the classic way to lose them.

## A two-hour plan

Two hours is one full game day. That means one Dagon's Breach window and one raid schedule are both inside the session, and the day's combat Marks (150) can be filled by a gate plus a raid.

1. Spend the first stretch on the capped daily list: combat Marks, a court writ if you hold the material, the bank exchange if you have Marks.
2. Use the middle on one progress goal — a questline step, a dungeon with a private instance, or profession gathering before the day's node slots turn.
3. Watch the clock for the event you actually want; do not try to catch every event.
4. Return to town, sell, and close safely.

> [!tip] The cap is not the session
> Reaching an account cap stops that reward; it does not stop play. A capped player can still gain skill, character level, profession XP, dungeon loot and quest progress. Decide which of those the session is for.

## What not to plan around

- A fixed Motherlode hour. The source sets a schedule of windows and warnings, not one published start time per lode.
- A letter while you are away from town. The courier needs you outdoors in a town by day; a step that needs a building waits for a town that has one.
- Loot from a respawn timer. Dungeon respawns are world clocks; someone else may clear the room before you return.
- A trip you cannot reverse. Check the return leg before you spend the session's time on the outward journey.

## Common mistakes

- Checking the caps after the activity. Read the account list first; otherwise you spend an hour on a reward that was already spent.
- Treating a world timer as a personal allowance. A dungeon respawn clock is not a daily cap, and a capped account still has uncapped progress.
- Planning a route by distance alone. The route planner prices roads cheapest and open ground dearest, so a longer road route can be faster; see Overworld travel.
- Forgetting the return. A one-way trip can fit while the session cannot.

## Next

- Catching up in short sessions
- Caps, timers and resets

docs.title: The progression map
docs.summary: How character level, Renown, Firmament stars, gear, professions and companions depend on each other.
headings: How the tracks feed each other
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Two ladders run at once: character level from your skills, and Renown (1 to 50) from online activity.
> - Character level opens questlines and gives a fixed pool of attribute points; Renown supplies 2 Firmament stars per level after the first.
> - Renown opens elite foes at Renown 5 and revenants at 10.
> - Gear and the Firmament must keep up with the threat, which grows after character level 10 and Renown 15.
> - Only two crafts may pass Journeyman, and masteries are permanent: those are the long-term commitments.

## The six tracks

DFO Online does not have one experience bar. Six tracks advance in parallel, and each pays into the others.

| Track | What raises it | What it gives | Gate or limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Character level | Uses of your class skills; the game checks about every six game hours | Health and attribute points; opens questlines | Questline steps open at set levels |
| Renown | Kills, quests, parties, raids, gates, writs and other witnessed acts | Health and spell points, Firmament stars, and system unlocks | 50 levels; 15000 XP per account-hour |
| Firmament | Renown pays Stars; profession ranks pay Craft points | Passive bonuses along one path, capped by channel | Refunds; whole-sky respec |
| Gear | Loot, crafting, quest reward cards and reforging | Damage, armour, techniques and affixes | Loot rarity; tier and material rules |
| Professions | Gathering and crafting work | Materials, goods, writ pay, Craft points | Two crafts above rank 50 |
| Companions | Spare a defeated revenant, then loyalty and levels | A second fighter with its own sky | Revenants begin at Renown 10 |

The level-up numbers behind each row are explained on Levelling online and Renown.

## How the tracks feed each other

- Character level → questlines. Every introduction line opens at a character level (2, 3, 4, 5, and so on), so the fastest way to meet a system is to level normally. See The questline ladder.
- Renown → stars and unlocks. Each Renown level after the first pays 2 Stars. Renown 5 opens your own-world elites, Renown 10 opens revenants and companions, and Renown 10 is also the founding requirement for a player guild. See Renown and Elites and champions.
- Professions → stars. Craft points come from the sum of your profession ranks: one Craft point per eight ranks, capped per track. Craft points buy life-ring stars only; they never buy combat stars. See The Firmament.
- Renown and level → threat. Foes gain health and damage from character level 11 upward, then from Renown 16 upward, compounding. That is why a fast level on weak gear makes the game harder, not easier. See The hero's threat.
- Companions → Renown. Companions are a Renown 10 system; their own sky and loyalty are separate from yours. See Companions.

## What to do first

The order that wastes the least is:

1. Keep your class skills in use. Character level is the key to the introduction lines, and each level gives a fixed attribute pool online (see Levelling online).
2. Pick one or two crafts you will actually use. A combat character usually wants a repair craft and a supply craft; a caster or hybrid may want Enchanting. Do not spread ranks across three crafts you intend to pass 50 — two is the permanent limit.
3. Earn Renown through capped activities. Events and quests pay Renown at a rate; quests also open the systems. The hourly cap is per account, so short sessions and long sessions converge.
4. Spend stars on the offence you already use. A damage channel is capped, so a tree that feeds one weapon family, one spell school or fists goes further than a scattered one. Fill the offence then the defence budgets.
5. Replace gear instead of protecting it. The threat grows; a found or quested piece at your tier is worth more than a repaired old one.
6. At Renown 10, start the companion track only after you have a reliable fight and a bank buffer.

## The permanent decisions

Some choices are cheap to change and some are not.

- Firmament: refunds are free below Renown 10; after that they cost 10 Marks a star, and the whole-sky respec costs 10000 gold.
- Crafts: only 2 crafts may rise above Journeyman (rank 50). A third is held at rank 50.
- Masteries: chosen when a skill reaches 100, and a mastery can never be undone. You have two primary, two major and one minor slot.
- Creation: race, class, biography and a custom class's restrictions have no general undo; race and class are not editable later. See Choices that are hard to undo.

## Common mistakes

- Rushing level on weak gear. Threat grows with level, so the character who levels fastest without gear or stars meets the hardest version of every fight.
- Treating Renown as a second experience bar. It is a separate ladder with its own cap and its own rewards; character level does not raise it directly.
- Spending craft ranks on three crafts. The service holds the third at rank 50; the earlier two are the pair you keep.
- Choosing a mastery before planning the slots. Masteries are permanent, and a build that needs two primary masteries should not spend a primary slot elsewhere.
- Ignoring the Firmament's group caps. A second star in a full channel adds nothing; check the shared cap before buying deeper.

## Next

- Levelling online
- Renown

docs.title: Renown
docs.summary: Online's own ladder from 1 to 50: what earns it, its caps, and what it unlocks.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Renown is a separate, online-only level kept for each character by the account service.
> - Earn Renown XP from eligible kills, quests, parties and several shared activities.
> - Every source pays 75% of its full-rate amount; an account can receive at most 15000 XP per real hour.
> - Renown adds online Health and Spell Points and opens systems at set thresholds.

## A second level

Renown runs from level 1 to 50. It does not replace character level: your Daggerfall skills still
determine character-level progress, while Renown tracks online progression. The account service keeps one Renown
track per character and supplies the authoritative level. Offline play does not earn or apply Renown.

## What earns Renown

You earn XP when you defeat eligible foes or finish quests. Your foe or quest level is read no more than three levels
above your current Renown, so high-level content cannot skip the early curve. The kill reward is shared with players
who struck the foe recently. A party adds a bonus per eligible member present; each player earns XP rather than
sharing a single pool.

The service also credits certain witnessed activities: defending a town raid, defeating the Sea Serpent, winning Arena
bouts, holding Starfall stars, and filling court writs. These awards follow their own event rules and are subject to
the same account-wide hourly cap.

> [!online] XP rate and cap
> Each source pays 75% of its full-rate XP, rounded down. One account can receive no more than
> 15000 XP in a real clock hour across its characters. A second character does not provide a
> second allowance. The service does not keep XP above that cap for later.

## What Renown changes

Each Renown level after the first adds 3 maximum Health and 2 maximum Spell Points while you play online. The bonus
adjusts with the level and disappears offline; the underlying character save remains separate.

Renown also opens later systems. Your own-world elite spawns begin at Renown 5. Revenants are held until Renown 10.
The Firmament grants stars as your Renown rises, and other later systems have their own gates.

## Common mistakes

- Counting the hourly cap per character. It belongs to the account and is shared across its characters.
- Assuming the cap stores overflow. XP beyond the limit in that clock hour is not banked.
- Reading Renown as character level. The two tracks advance for different reasons.

## Next

a-second-level.title: A second level
a-second-level.excerpt: Renown runs from level 1 to 50. It does not replace character level: your Daggerfall skills still determine character-level progress, while Renown tracks online progression. The account service keeps one Renown track per character and supplies the authoritative level. Offline play does not earn or apply Renown.

what-earns-renown.title: What earns Renown
what-earns-renown.excerpt: You earn XP when you defeat eligible foes or finish quests. Your foe or quest level is read no more than three levels above your current Renown, so high-level content cannot skip the early curve. The kill reward is shared with players who struck the foe recently. A party adds a bonus per eligible member present; each player earns XP rather than sharing a single pool.

what-renown-changes.title: What Renown changes
what-renown-changes.excerpt: Each Renown level after the first adds 3 maximum Health and 2 maximum Spell Points while you play online. The bonus adjusts with the level and disappears offline; the underlying character save remains separate.

docs.title: The Firmament
docs.summary: The Firmament's signs, paths and two point pools, and how to spend and refund them.
headings: The opening route: pause, Growth, Firmament
Caps: why more of the same stops helping
What to spend points on first
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Open it from the pause menu's Growth tab. Written in the Stars introduces it at character level 3 online, and the service needs a registered account.
> - Choose one of seven starts, then buy only stars connected to what you already hold. A keystone can be reached but not passed through.
> - Renown supplies Stars for the combat sky; profession ranks supply Craft points for the life ring only.
> - Below Renown 10, refunds are free. From Renown 10 each refunded Star costs 10 Marks; a whole-sky respec costs 10,000 gold.
> - Every channel and every group has a cap, so stacking one damage bonus stops helping.

## The opening route: pause, Growth, Firmament

The Firmament is a tree of passive bonuses held by the account service, so it works online only. Open the pause menu and choose the Growth tab. That tab also holds Level and Specialisations; the Firmament section draws the sky. Press Accept to keep a change.

The introduction questline Written in the Stars opens at character level 3 for online play. It teaches the choice of a sign; the tree itself is read in the Growth tab. The service needs a registered account to store the allocation.

## Two purses

Firmament point purses and a connected branch ending at a keystone

Renown gives Stars: 2 for every Renown level after the first, so 18 at Renown 10 and 98 at Renown 50.

Craft points come from professions. The law sums your ranks across the ten profession tracks, counts each track at most 100, and gives 1 Craft point per 8 total ranks. Ten rank-100 tracks therefore give 125 Craft points. Craft points buy life-ring stars only; they can never buy a blow, a spell or a ward.

When a life star is bought, the game spends Craft points first and any remaining Stars after. Spending a Star on the life ring is therefore a real choice, not an automatic one.

## Starts and paths

There are seven free starts: The Mage, The Shadow, The Thief, The Steed, The Warrior, The Ritual, and The Serpent in the middle. The six signs surround the inner ring; the Serpent reaches all six. A start is where a path begins, not a class or a build.

Allocate only a star that is one line from your start or from a star you already hold. Select a distant star and the window previews the shortest route and charges for every missing star on it. A keystone ends its path: you can own it, but you cannot buy past it to another star. Cross-links join some branches so you can enter sideways.

The sky names its tiers small, notable and keystone. Every non-start star costs one point whatever its tier or ring. Small stars tend to one focused bonus; notables combine several; a combat keystone gives a larger benefit with a cost, while a life keystone has no negative stat.

## Caps: why more of the same stops helping

Each channel has a maximum the whole sky may add, listed in the law's STATDEFS. Common ones: one weapon-family damage channel at most 30%, a combat skill at most +15 points, an attribute +15, evasion a 10% chance, armour 10, maximum Health 75, blows taken at most 30% less, and spell-cost reduction 25%.

The blow and the cast are then capped again as groups when they are read. The ordinary weapon channels of one blow are capped together at +30%, with a −20% floor; the whole blow, including conditional bonuses such as an unaware foe, is capped at +50%. A keystone's drawback is paid after its benefit has been capped, so it cannot be hidden by the cap.

## Refunds and the respec

A refund is free below Renown 10. At that Renown and above, every refunded Star costs 10 Marks. The charge counts every star removed, including a connecting star's dependents: taking a link back also takes any star that no longer reaches your start through what remains.

Your first sign is free. Changing it refunds the old tree and charges for the stars taken back at the same rate.

The whole-sky respec is a separate action. It clears your sign and every allocated star for 10000 gold whatever your Renown, without the Marks charge. Share codes carry a tree between players, but a code made under a different version of the sky is refused rather than misread.

## What to spend points on first

Find the wedge that matches the offence you already use: a spell school, a weapon family, fists or archery. Buy outward along that path toward its notable and its keystone. A keystone is a trade, so read its drawback before you commit.

Do not open a second damage branch until you have checked the shared group caps. Once the blow or cast group is full, points usually go further in defence: blows taken, armour, maximum Health and regeneration each have a separate budget. Attributes and combat skills are small per point but feed every formula behind an attack and a defence, so they rarely waste a point.

Spend Craft points on the life-ring stars for the professions you actually rank — yield and experience first, then carry weight or travel fatigue. Craft points arrive slowly, so plan the order.

## When the sky sleeps

The Firmament is in force while you are online and have chosen a sign. It sleeps offline and while mentoring. Its combat channels also sleep in refereed duels and Arena bouts, and the sky never raises damage against another player.

The life channels — gathering, prices, carry, travel fatigue — work in ordinary online play, because there is no fight in a price. In a siege and in the Wrothgarian open zone the combat channels still work against NPC foes, but a strike or spell aimed at a player is rolled with the sky taken off.

## Common mistakes

- Buying toward a distant star without reading the route. You pay for every missing star the preview shows.
- Treating a keystone as a free bonus. Its drawback counts against the same channel and group caps as its benefit.
- Spending Craft points on combat. They cannot buy combat stars.
- Refunding after Renown 10 without counting the cascade. A connecting star takes its dependents with it, and each is charged.
- Assuming the sky works everywhere. It sleeps offline, while mentoring, and in duels and Arena bouts.

## Next

- Renown
- Craft specialisations

docs.title: Professions
docs.summary: The ten gathering and crafting tracks, introduced by The Court Crafter.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A registered account can begin The Court Crafter at character level 2.
> - Five gathering tracks and five craft tracks cover collecting materials and making goods.
> - You may raise every gathering track, but only 2 craft tracks may rise above Journeyman (rank 50).
> - Use Professions to review progress and Stores to manage materials for later work.

## The tracks

The gathering tracks are Mining, Logging, Herbalism, Hunting and Fishing. Craft tracks are Smithing, Building, Outfitting, Provisioning and Enchanting. A recipe may name a discipline within a craft: Jewelcrafting work, for example, raises Smithing; Cooking and Alchemy work raise Provisioning. This distinction matters when you choose specialisations later.

Each track advances from Novice through Apprentice, Journeyman and Expert to Master. Higher ranks open more material and recipe tiers. Gathering and crafting use separate tracks from your character's ordinary skills.

## Begin the introduction

At level 2, look for The Court Crafter, offered online by a court crafter. Its introduction asks you to find materials and make something. Profession work is an online account service, so a guest account cannot take the line or use the profession book; access also depends on the service being open.

Open Professions from the pause menu's Stats rail to see the gathering and craft tracks. Stores shows stored materials and the work actions available to you. Crafting can draw from Stores and from materials you carry in your pack or Materials Bag.

> [!online] Online rule
> Professions and Stores are DFO Online systems. Daggerfall Unity alone does not have these profession tracks. The account service is authoritative for profession operations and material changes.

## Plan for later

Gathering has its own nodes, climates and daily availability; see Gathering. Crafting turns materials into goods at workstations; see Crafting. At Journeyman, consider which crafts you want to keep advancing before committing to ranks above it. The rank-50 and rank-100 choices are covered in Craft specialisations.

## Next

- Gathering
- Crafting

- The progression map

docs.title: Gathering
docs.summary: Nodes, climates, daily slots, seasons and Tides.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Gather from world nodes with the matching profession: Mining, Logging, Herbalism, Hunting or Fishing.
> - Climate shapes which land nodes and herbs appear; the same map pixel shares its daily node layout.
> - The node calendar follows UTC days. Season and Tide effects can change what a harvest yields.
> - There is no general daily harvest-count cap in this source snapshot; availability, specific limits and service rules still apply.

## Find the right work

Mining, Logging and Herbalism use veins, trees and herb patches in the land. Their availability depends on the climate of the map pixel, and herb types vary by climate. The daily node layout is deterministic and shared, so other players encounter the same basic nodes there. If a patch is unfamiliar, the map's climate and your profession page help explain what you can work.

Fishing uses a net haul, while Hunting harvests witnessed creature remains. These are different actions from clicking a land node, but they use the same profession system and award materials and profession experience.

## Work the calendar

The gathering day follows UTC. Herb availability and yield may change with the season: some plants are seasonal, and winter can leave certain plants bare. A map pixel's herb patch is initially conservative about its tier until enough reports agree on its identity.

Weekly Tides can also affect yields. A Harvest Tide improves land-gathering yields, Blight reduces herb and wood yields, and Storm Season improves fishing haul yields. These are shared calendar conditions; check the current Tide before planning a long gathering run.

## Rank and limits

Your rank determines which tiers you can work. A clean harvest gives more profession experience. Working a node far below the highest tier your rank has opened awards less experience, so moving to appropriate-tier sources helps your profession advance.

The law has no general daily cap on harvest count in this snapshot. Specific limits still exist, including a daily limit on high-tier hides, while nodes can be exhausted for the UTC day and the account service limits operation rates. Do not treat the absence of a general cap as unlimited access to every material.

Collected materials can feed the Crafting stations or remain in Stores for future orders and Court writs.

## Next

- Crafting
- Money and markets

docs.title: Crafting
docs.summary: Stations, recipes, quality odds and profession ranks.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Open Professions and choose a craft to see available work and recipes.
> - A recipe draws its inputs from Stores and the materials in your pack or Materials Bag.
> - Recipe tier and your craft rank affect the quality roll; specialisation choices can shift particular outcomes.
> - Craft disciplines can share a track. For example, Jewelcrafting raises Smithing, while Cooking raises Provisioning.

## Gather, then work

Crafting uses the five craft tracks: Smithing, Building, Outfitting, Provisioning and Enchanting. Some recipes belong to a discipline within one of these tracks. That discipline names the work, but its shared craft track is where rank and experience accrue.

Use Stores to review materials you have deposited, then choose a recipe or work action in the profession pages. Stations include the Forge, Workbench, Loom, mason's bench and jeweller's bench. Alchemy and Enchanting work is also available through the profession service. The page explains when a station is unavailable or lacks what the recipe needs.

The Materials Bag is a portable way to carry crafting materials. Stations can draw from it as well as from Stores and your carried pack items. Check the recipe's inputs before leaving town so you know what to gather or withdraw.

## Quality and rank

Crafted quality ranges from Crude through Standard, Fine and Superior to Masterwork. Your rank relative to the recipe's rank sets the starting odds; a wide rank advantage makes higher quality more likely. Recipe rules and some specialisations can further shift the result. The displayed result is a roll, so a suitable rank improves your chances without guaranteeing a specific quality.

Higher tiers open as your profession rank rises. You can learn how node availability supports those recipes in Gathering. Above Journeyman, only a limited number of craft tracks can keep advancing; Craft specialisations explains the lasting choices.

## Next

- Gathering
- Craft specialisations

docs.title: Money and markets
docs.summary: Marks and other currencies, daily caps, the global market and court writs.
headings: Buy and sell on the Market
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Gold belongs to your character's save; Marks are held by your registered account.
> - The Bank of the Empire exchanges Marks for gold at 8 gold per Mark, up to 300 Marks per UTC day. The exchange is one-way.
> - A Market listing costs a 1% fee, rounded up with a minimum of 1 Mark; a sale then loses 5% tax, rounded down, and any seat Tithe.
> - Court writs trade requested materials from Stores for Marks and profession experience.

## Gold and Marks are different

Gold is carried and saved with your character. Marks sit in the account ledger, where DFO can award them for witnessed activity and bounded gathering or loot finds. At the Bank of the Empire, you can exchange Marks for gold; the exchange goes one way. The source defines no gold-to-Marks conversion. The Marks service and the Bank both need a registered account.

The Bank pays less than a Mark's own yardstick: the record values a Mark at about 10 gold of play, while the Bank pays 8. That spread is the price of turning account currency into carryable gold, and the 300-Mark daily cap keeps it slow.

Different Marks sources have their own limits. Combat rewards share a daily account cap, and gather and loot finds each have separate daily bounds. See Caps and timers for the handbook's broader cap reference, and Making money for what pays.

## Buy and sell on the Market

The Market handles listings and buy orders in Marks. You can list eligible materials or items; a local buyer receives a purchase immediately, while a buyer in another region pays courier costs and waits for delivery. The live board shows current offers; do not assume another player's asking price is a fixed value.

| Rule | What it costs |
|---|---|
| Listing fee | 1% of the listing's whole worth, rounded up, at least 1 Mark; burnt when you post, and not returned if you cancel |
| Sale tax | 5% of the sale, rounded down |
| Seat Tithe | The holding player guild's rate, where a guild holds the seat: 0–10% at a Palace, 0–15% at a Crown, with a Market Hall raising the cap a point per tier |
| Courier | By the load: ceil((units/20) × (1 + pixels/25)) Marks, at least 2; delivery takes 15 minutes plus a minute for every 10 pixels begun |
| Listing lifetime | 72 hours, up to 30 live listings an account |

The seller receives the price minus the tax and any Tithe. The tax is worked out on the running total of a listing, so selling a stack a unit at a time does not avoid it. There is no Tithe where no seat holds the board's bailiwick; the seat rules are on City control.

> [!example] A 100-Mark sale
> You list goods worth 100 Marks. The listing fee is 1 Mark (1% of 100, rounded up), so you pay 1 Mark to post. If the whole listing sells, the tax is 5% of 100, or 5 Marks. With no seat Tithe the seller collects 95 Marks; a 10% Palace Tithe would take a further 10, leaving 85. The buyer pays the listed price either way.

Access requires a registered account and the Market, professions and Marks services to be open. Buy orders live 7 days, up to 20 an account.

## Fill a Court writ

The Work tab offers Court writs for requested materials. Fill one by delivering the requested quantity from your Stores; the writ pays Marks based on the material's value and adds profession experience. You can complete up to 3 writs per UTC day. Gathering materials for a writ is one way to connect the Professions and economy systems.

> [!note] Other tokens
> Soul Cakes, Weir Keys and Welkynd Shards have separate uses and accounting. They are not general substitutes for gold or Marks.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the listing fee is burnt. Cancel a listing and the fee stays spent; the goods come back, the Mark does not.
- Splitting a sale to dodge tax. The tax is charged on the running total, so unit-by-unit sales pay the same.
- Assuming every board takes a Tithe. It applies only where a player guild holds the seat that covers the board.
- Expecting to buy Marks with gold. The Bank exchanges one way only.

## Next

- Making money
- Gathering

docs.title: Making money
docs.summary: What actually pays in DFO Online, the rates the source sets, and the routes that pay poorly.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A full bounty pack of eight pays 50 gold in tier 1 (levels 1–3), 75 in tier 2, 90 in tier 3, 100 in tier 4 and 190–200 in tier 5 (level 15+).
> - A counter pays at most half what it would ask its best haggler, so vendoring is steady but slow.
> - Court writs pay Marks, up to 3 a UTC day; combat Marks share a 150-a-day cap and exchange for gold at 8 each.
> - The market can beat a counter, but charges a 1% listing fee, a 5% sale tax and sometimes a seat's Tithe.

## Two purses, one exchange

Gold is carried with the character; Marks are held by the registered account and spent on the market, guild seats and star refunds. The Bank of the Empire sells Marks for gold at 8 gold each, up to 300 Marks a UTC day, and never the other way. See Money and markets.

## Quests and their reward tiers

A quest pays what its script says, then the questline layer scales the gold by the outcome's factor, bounded between 0.75 and 1.5, and offers three fitted gear choices at the quest's tier: tiers 1–2 start at Magic, tiers 3–4 at Rare, and no tier's floor is Legendary. No universal per-level reward exists, so read the card. Introduction steps pay 100–200 gold for the level 2–4 lines and 200–400 for the level 5 and 6 lines, the scripts' own ranges.

## Notice-board bounties

Each town board posts four hunts a game day; a character holds four, and a taken bounty lapses after a game day. The purse depends on the monster tier and the pack size:

| Bounty tier | Levels | Full pack of eight |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1–3 | 50 gold |
| 2 | 4–5 | 75 gold |
| 3 | 6–10 | 90 gold |
| 4 | 11–14 | 100 gold |
| 5 | 15+ | 190–200 gold |

A surface pack runs four to eight beasts, and each one short of eight takes a tenth off the full purse, so four pay 60%. A dungeon pack of two to four is valued as a surface pack of four, six or eight. Each bounty also pays a kit piece: half condition and never Magic below level 4, three-quarter condition and half Magic at 4–5, and full condition and the same chance from level 6.

## Gathering, crafting and ranks

The ten tracks run 0–100, and rank n takes 10 × n² experience: Journeyman (50) is 25,000 and Master 100,000. Only two crafts may pass Journeyman. Materials list at a price you choose and earn whatever a buyer agrees; the market sets no price of its own. Harvests also roll a Mark find — a 10% chance of 2–5 Marks, capped at 30 an account a day — and bodies, piles and searches roll 1–4 Marks at 5%, 12% and 15%, capped at 20. Crafted gear tops out at Masterwork, about one Rare roll, so world loot usually sells better than the anvil.

## Counter or market

An NPC counter buys eligible loot at once. Its offer starts from the item's value, quality, condition and the counter's quality, and online the sale is capped at half the counter's best-haggler ask; Mercantile and Personality move you under that ceiling. A found piece sells at its found condition, your own repairs add a third and a smith's paid repair adds nothing.

The market reaches other players. Listings last 72 hours and an account may keep 30 live. Posting costs a 1% fee, at least 1 Mark; a sale pays 5% tax and may owe a seat's Tithe of 0–10%, or 0–15% under a crown seat. A buyer in another region pays a courier fee and waits. Compare the net; the fee is kept if the listing is cancelled.

## Court writs and Marks

Court writs take materials from Stores and pay units × material Mark value × 1.2, up to 3 writs a UTC day, with profession experience and Renown. Guild writs pay from a guild's Marks treasury, need the listed material, and pay at most 1.5 times its Mark value. Combat pays Marks too: a Dagon's Breach gate 50, a defended town raid 30, a sea serpent 40 (20 to a ship that did not stand half the fight), an Elite Breach Redoubt 20, a held fallen star 30 and a Motherlode 10. They share a 150-Mark ceiling per account per UTC day, paid down to it rather than lost. At the bank the day's exchange is worth at most 2,400 gold.

## What pays poorly

- Vendoring common loot. The half-price ceiling makes a counter a steady trickle, not a plan.
- Repairing before selling. A smith's paid repair adds no sale credit, and your own adds a third.
- Fighting past the combat cap. After 150 Marks in a UTC day, gates and raids stop paying until the reset.

## Common mistakes

- Counting the bank exchange as income. It converts Marks you already earned; it does not create gold.
- Treating bounty gold as the reward. The gear roll and the Renown are often worth more than the purse.

## Next

- Money and markets
- Notice boards

- Choosing a money route

Combat pays Marks too: a Dagon's Breach gate 50, a defended town raid 30, a sea serpent 40 (20 to a ship that did not stand half the fight), an Elite Breach Redoubt 20, a held fallen star 30 and a Motherlode 10. They share a 150-Mark ceiling per account per UTC day, paid down to it rather than lost. At the bank the day's exchange is worth at most 2,400 gold.

docs.title: Choosing a money route
docs.summary: Pick between quests, bounties, gathering, crafting, writs and the market by time, caps and opportunity cost.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Take the capped routes first: combat Marks (150 a UTC day), court writs (3), the bank exchange (300 Marks), then spend the rest of the session on an uncapped route.
> - A bounty is the most reliable early loop: one posting, one pack, gold plus a kit piece.
> - An NPC counter always pays at most half its best-haggler price, so vendoring is steady but slow.
> - The market can beat a counter but pays on a buyer's schedule, not yours, and charges a 1% fee and 5% tax.
> - The route's real cost is the trip: count the journey both ways before choosing it.

This page is about choosing between income routes. Making money has the full rates; the point here is what each route costs you in time, caps and risk.

## What each route is for

| Route | What it pays | Limit or cost | The catch | Best when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quests | Gold (the introduction steps pay 100–400), a gear choice, faction standing | One step at a time; travel to the giver | A step can wait an hour of character time for the next | You also want the questline's unlock |
| Bounties | 50 / 75 / 90 / 100 gold for a full pack in tiers 1–4, 190–200 in tier 5, plus a kit piece | Four postings per board per game day; a taken bounty lapses after one game day | The pack stands 4–10 map pixels away; the hunt is the trip | You want a predictable short outing |
| Combat events | Marks: gate 50, raid 30, serpent 40, Redoubt 20, star 30; gold and loot | 150 Marks per account per UTC day across all of them | The window is short and world-scheduled | The event is already near |
| Court writs | Marks equal to units × the material's Mark value × 1.2, plus profession XP and Renown | 3 writs per UTC day | Needs the material already in Stores | You already hold the material |
| Gathering | Materials at whatever a buyer pays, plus a 10% chance of 2–5 Marks per harvest (30 a day) | Node slots reset daily; travel to climates | No fixed material price exists | You are passing the nodes anyway |
| Crafting | Crafted goods at market prices; profession ranks; writ materials | Rank n costs 10 × n² XP; only two crafts above rank 50 | Long payback, and the market may not buy | You need the craft anyway |
| Market | A player's price minus a 1% listing fee, 5% tax and any Tithe | 72-hour listing; 30 live | A buyer must want it at your price | The good is wanted and you can wait |
| Vendoring | At most half the counter's best-haggler ask | None | Immediate but capped | You have spare loot and no plan for it |
| Bank exchange | 8 gold per Mark | 300 Marks per UTC day, one way | Converts Marks you already earned | You have surplus Marks |

## Three rules of opportunity cost

1. Count the round trip. A hunt four map pixels away and one twenty pixels away can pay the same; the nearer one costs less of the session. The route planner prices roads cheapest and open ground dearest, so the shortest line is not always the fastest trip (Overworld travel).
2. Caps are account-wide, not per activity. Once the day's 150 combat Marks are paid, another gate adds no Marks; the same is true of the Renown hour and the writ count. Switch routes rather than repeat a capped one.
3. Carried takings are at risk. An ordinary death takes one tenth of the gold you carry, and Open Zone death can expose carried items and cart contents. Bank before the risky leg, not after.

## A concrete early loop

This is an example of the arithmetic, not a guaranteed rate:

1. Start in a town. Take a board bounty whose target is close, and note the one-game-day life of a taken posting.
2. Do the hunt. A tier-1 full pack of eight pays 50 gold; a four-beast pack pays 60% of the full purse (30). The pack also drops a kit piece at your level.
3. Return and sell. Keep usable gear, sell the spares at the counter and salvage Magic-or-better only if you need shards. A counter offer is immediate but capped at half its best-haggler price.
4. Bank the gold. Keep a small traveling purse.
5. Repeat once. Two bounties plus an introduction step (100–200 gold) is roughly 200–400 gold before loot, which is a useful start on training, repairs and a Portal Stone's five shards.
6. Convert Marks if you have them. The bank pays 8 gold a Mark, up to 300 Marks a day; the exchange never goes the other way.

## Choosing by session length

- Under half an hour: stay in the same region. A bounty plus a counter sale is the simplest loop; skip anything with a long approach.
- About an hour: one bounty and one introduction quest step, or a nearby event window and a sell.
- Two hours: one full game day. Take the capped rewards (combat Marks, a writ if you hold the material, the bank exchange), then one progress goal. Events can fill the gap between windows.

## What not to do

- Grinding kills past the caps. Renown stops paying at 15000 XP per account-hour and combat Marks stop at 150 a day; kills still give loot and skill, but not those currencies.
- Taking a bounty you cannot finish. A taken posting lapses after one game day, about two real hours, and the kills do not carry to a fresh posting on another day.
- Repairing before selling. A smith's paid repair adds no sale credit and your own repairs credit a third; sell as found.
- Listing without reading the net. Fee, tax and Tithe can leave less than the counter offered; the fee is kept if you cancel.
- Treating the bank exchange as profit. It converts Marks you already earned; it does not create gold.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing the highest-paying route instead of the one you can reach. Travel can consume the whole session.
- Taking a capped reward last. If the cap turns mid-session, the reward you planned is gone for the day.
- Carrying the session's takings back. Bank at the first counter, not at the last one.

## Next

- Making money
- Money and markets

docs.title: Wagons and hauling
docs.summary: Carts and wagons, their upkeep, and The Merchant's Road.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A cart or wagon is a pack item that you deploy behind you to carry goods.
> - The Small Cart, Open Wagon and Caravan differ in capacity, horse team and whether passengers can ride.
> - Buy enough horses to hitch the wagon; you can buy additional horses at a Stable.
> - The level-3 introduction The Merchant's Road begins with a stable master.

## Choose a wagon

The Small Cart is the lightest option. The Open Wagon carries more and has passenger seats. The Caravan carries the most and opens as an enterable room. Check the Stable's listing and your carrying needs before buying; each type requires its own horse team, bought separately.

Your wagon is represented by an item in your pack. Deploying it places it behind you, where it carries goods you would otherwise carry yourself. It is not a way to travel instantly between towns. If you own multiple kinds, the wagon law selects the best one to drive.

## Wear and care

Travel wears a wagon. Road and off-road movement, load and wagon type affect the wear. A Wagon Yard can repair it, and a Wagon Repair Kit lets you mend it in the field. Your wagon upkeep tier affects what its condition means for pace and sale value. Boons is the default tier, but upkeep is a player-controlled online setting; check your current setting before assuming wear slows your wagon.

Park with care in towns. The online wagon warden can move teams that linger on roads or exceed a town's parking allowance; the wagon and its cargo remain yours at the relocation point.

## Take the introduction

At character level 3, a stable master can offer The Merchant's Road, a short introduction to moving a wagon's load and completing a haul. It is a good point to learn how the job's cargo and route fit your normal travel. See Horses for riding and Overworld travel for journeys between places.

## Next

- Tavern games
- Horses

docs.title: Tavern games
docs.summary: The games A Seat at the Table introduces.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A Seat at the Table opens with a tavern regular at character level 2.
> - Its second step introduces The King's Gambit, a card-table game of armies and kings.
> - The King's Gambit is enabled by default, but you can switch it off for your own game.
> - When it is off, tables offer Hold'em and Iliac Hand instead.

## Find the tables

Taverns are places to rest and meet other players, and their card tables host online games. A Seat at the Table is a short introduction questline from a tavern regular. Its first step is A Hand of Cards; its second, The King's Gambit, waits until the King's Gambit feature is enabled.

The King's Gambit is a game of armies and kings at a tavern card table. You can play against a regular or another player, for gold or for fun. If you do not see the table, check the feature's setting: it is on by default, but it remains your own setting online. With it off, tables offer Hold'em and Iliac Hand.

## Next

docs.title: The hero's threat
docs.summary: How the world grows tougher as your level and Renown rise.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Foes gain health and deal more damage as your character level rises above 10.
> - Renown adds a second, compounding increase above Renown 15.
> - The character-level steps are larger than the Renown steps.
> - The scaling stops counting character levels above 30 and Renown above 50.

## Two tracks shape the threat

The hero's threat system gives newly built foes more health and stronger blows as your character level and Renown
rise. Online, its Loot Rarity feature gate is forced on. It uses both tracks
independently, then multiplies their effects together. Below character level 10 and Renown
15, neither track adds threat.

| Track | First level that adds threat | Each step adds to foe health | Each step adds to foe damage | Last level counted |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Character level | 11 | 4% | 7% | 30 |
| Renown | 16 | 0.5% | 1% | 50 |

The increases compound. For example, the next character level multiplies the current threat again; it does not add a
fixed number of Health points. Levels beyond each track's last counted level add no more from that track.

This scaling is checked when a foe is built. A shared foe keeps its owner's health result; a visitor's own level does
not rebuild that foe's Health. The visitor's damage scaling still applies to blows dealt by the shared foe.

## What this means for you

Growing stronger also changes the fights the world gives you. A higher level can make an old kind of foe tougher, and
Renown contributes even when your character level has stopped rising. This does not mean every foe is individually
matched to you: the threat factor scales a foe's health and damage, while other systems decide which foes appear and
their base level.

See Levelling online for character levels and Renown for its separate track.

## Common mistakes

- Expecting threat to stop at character level 10. That is where level scaling begins.
- Expecting Renown to replace character level. Its increase is separate and compounds with the level-based one.
- Assuming your level changes a shared foe's Health. The source makes its Health owner-authoritative in shared
  play; the visiting player's threat affects its damage only.

## Next

- Renown
- Elites and champions

docs.title: Loot rarity
docs.summary: Rarity tiers, materials, item lines and sets, introduced by The Smith's Secrets.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Online Loot Rarity is active from your first eligible drop; The Smith's Secrets introduces the gear systems at level 4.
> - Magic, Rare and Legendary are the tiers the rarity ladder rolls.
> - Aetheric gear comes from set sources, Artifacts are Daggerfall's own, and Gilded gear is a fixed unique spoil.
> - Read a piece's card: its tier, affix lines, sockets and identification state all matter.

## The rarity ladder

The ladder contains seven tiers. The middle three are generated by the rarity system; the other tiers have distinct
sources and should not be read as another random drop rank.

| Tier | What the tier means |
|---|---|
| Common | Plain gear without the rarity ladder's added affixes. |
| Magic | One or two added affixes, or Daggerfall's own magic item. |
| Rare | Three or four affixes, a generated name and a catalogue enchantment. |
| Legendary | A fixed named record with its signature affixes and enchantment. |
| Aetheric | Set gear from its designated boss or the Sigil Broker; not rolled by the rarity ladder. |
| Artifact | Daggerfall's own artifacts. |
| Gilded | A fixed, unique spoil; not a random rarity roll. |

Affixes add readable effects such as damage, armour, attributes, resistance, skills or carrying capacity. The item card
shows these lines when identified. Some magic effects work before identification, but the added lines remain hidden
until you identify the item.

## Material and rarity are different

Online, Loot Rarity and Unleveled Loot both affect what you find. Loot Rarity determines the item's tier and added
lines. Unleveled Loot determines the material of random weapons and armour from factors such as Luck, shop quality and
dungeon kind; it does not use your character level to select the material. The online lane holds this mod to its
shipped defaults. A material name therefore does not tell you an item's rarity, and a rarity label does not determine
its material.

## Finding and reading a piece

Generic item-card fields to inspect before comparing gear

Check the tier label and item card before you compare gear. Rare and Legendary pieces can arrive unidentified; use an
Identify service to reveal their rolled lines. Online, the Reforge is available through the Mages Guild's Identify
service. It handles socket work and later improvements too; see Sockets and reforging.

The Smith's Secrets introduction opens at character level 4. Its steps require Loot Rarity to be on; online the
port forces that feature on. It introduces the system rather than unlocking the first rarity drop. See the
questline ladder for its giver and other gates.

> [!online] Sources of the tier
> Ordinary drops, set pieces and artifacts do not all use the same roll. Aetheric, Artifact and Gilded entries on the
> ladder identify their special sources; they are not promises that each is available from every loot container.

## Common mistakes

- Treating material as an item tier. Material and rarity are separate rolls.
- Expecting all seven tiers to be random drops. Only Magic, Rare and Legendary are rolled by the ladder.
- Selling an unidentified piece by its name alone. Identify it to read its added lines before deciding what it is
  worth to you.

## Next

- Sockets and reforging
- Salvage and repair

docs.title: Sockets and reforging
docs.summary: Gems, sockets and reforging gear.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Identify a piece before socket work, honing or reforging it.
> - Sockets hold one gem. Setting or removing a gem is free, but removing it outside the Reforge destroys it.
> - Reforging rerolls one eligible affix; honing raises one affix within its existing band.
> - The Reforge is part of the Mages Guild's Identify service.

## Sockets and gems

Some rarity gear has empty sockets. A short blade can hold one socket, a one-handed weapon two, and a two-handed
weapon three. Armour and jewellery can hold one. Magic weapons are limited to one; Rare and Legendary weapons may use
their full size. Other gear, such as clothing and ammunition, has no socket capacity.

Eight gem kinds are available: Ruby, Emerald, Sapphire, Diamond, Jade, Turquoise, Malachite and Amber. Each can be
Chipped, Flawed, plain, Flawless or Perfect. A gem's card shows the effect it grants; the effect depends on the gem,
its grade and whether it is set in a weapon or another item.

You can set a gem from your pack or at the Reforge, whether or not you are wearing the item. Setting and ordinary
unsetting are free. An unset gem shatters. Use Extract at the Reforge when you want to keep it: extraction has a
gold cost based on gem grade.

## Reforge and Hone

The Reforge rerolls one eligible line on a known Magic or Rare item, or the extra line on an Exalted Legendary.
The item must be identified and not worn. The cost depends on the rarity. A plain Legendary cannot be reforged, and
after the first reforge you can reroll only that same line again.

Hone raises one eligible line within its own band; it never lowers it. Each additional hone on the same piece
doubles its base cost. A gem's effect cannot be reforged or honed because it was not rolled as an affix.

These are choices with different trade-offs: reforge changes the value of a line, while hone improves a line you
already want. Compare the price on the item before committing materials.

> [!warning] Check what you are spending
> Reforging, honing and gem extraction use Welkynd Shards and gold. Salvage is the source of shards from eligible
> found gear; see Salvage and repair.

## Common mistakes

- Unsetting a gem when you mean to keep it. Ordinary removal shatters the gem; Extract returns it whole for gold.
- Trying to work on worn or unidentified gear. Identify first and remove the piece before reforge or hone.
- Expecting a Legendary item to reforge. Only an Exalted Legendary's extra line is eligible.

## Next

- Loot rarity
- Salvage and repair
