docs.title: Enchanting, spellmaking and potions
docs.summary: Turn gold, equipment and ingredients into custom magic, and distinguish guild makers from profession brewing.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Item making fits powers within an item's point budget; drawbacks make room without lowering the gold bill.
> - Spell making prices your chosen effects and separately shows the spell points needed to cast.
> - Profession brewing uses recipes, ingredients and rank, with ordinary and Potent results.
> - Guild halls and selected temples offer makers; profession Alchemy uses its own station route.

## Item making / enchanting

Open Make Magic Items at Mages Guild or Julianos rank 5. Select equipment, powers and side effects. Enchanted items are excluded except crafted jewellery, whose existing enchantments occupy points. Aetheric and Gilded pieces are refused.

Capacity is base + floor(base  material multiplier). Weapon/armor multipliers depend on metal; crafted jewellery can carry recipe-derived points.

Add chosen power costs and negative side-effect costs to find points used. Forced effects attached by a soul are excluded from this point sum. Gold is a different sum: power points  10, including forced powers, excluding drawbacks. Online Enchanting discounts gold by 10% at Journeyman and 20% at Master; Efficient adds 5 percentage points. Discounts round the final charge up.

The 24 types comprise 15 powers and nine drawbacks:

| Powers | Drawbacks |
|---|---|
| Absorbs Spells; Cast When Held; Cast When Strikes; Cast When Used; Enhances Skill; Extra Spell Pts; Feather Weight; Good Rep With; Improves Talents; Increased Weight Allowance; Potent Vs; Regens Health; Repairs Objects; Strengthens Armor; Vampiric Effect | Bad Reactions From; Bad Rep With; Extra Weight; Health Leech; Item Deteriorates; Low Damage Vs; Soul Bound; User Takes Damage; Weakens Armor |

Cast When Used activates a spell; Cast When Held applies worn magic with durability costs. Skill enhancement is a constant modifier. Strikes and damage-versus effects require weapons. Conflicting settings and duplicate drawbacks are excluded. Plan within ten rows, including forced effects; application has an eleven-row truncation quirk.

> [!example] Example: capacity and price
> Feather Weight costs 100 points. Extra Spell Pts during Winter costs 500. Together they use 600 points and cost 6,000 gold before discounts. Adding Item Deteriorates in holy places contributes -500, reducing used capacity to 100 while leaving the bill at 6,000. You accept the deterioration.

## Spell making

Open Make Spells as a Mages Guild member or at Kynareth rank 6. Carry a spellbook, choose effects, name the spell and pay. Three slots offer duration, chance or magnitude where supported. Targets must suit every effect.

For each supported component, gold is trunc(offset + A  base + B  trunc(increase / per-level)), with coefficients from that effect's cost table. Magnitude uses averaged minimum/maximum settings. Through skill 100, each effect's spell points are trunc(effect gold  (110 - school skill) / 400). Online above 100, use trunc(effect gold  10  100 / (skill  400)).

Sum effects, multiply both totals by target cost, then truncate: self/touch x1, single ranged x1.5, area around caster x2, area ranged x2.5. Normal casting has a five-point floor; player cost modifiers and free-cast effects can change the result. Chapter pricing also changes the purchase bill online. Check final totals, maximum magicka, target and scaling. The effect editor omits target multipliers and the floor. See Archery and magic.

## Potion making

There are 20 recipes. Guild Make Potions uses carried ingredients, including wagon and Materials Bag supplies, and makes one potion per successful mix. Its Recipes picker uses carried recipe items. Unmatched mixtures consume ingredients without producing anything.

Find this service at the Brotherhood or temples of Arkay, Akatosh, Dibella, Mara, Stendarr and Zenithar. Profession Alchemy instead uses Stores at an open alchemist's shop or licensed home/hall station.

Profession brewing charges 25 gold per brew plus ingredients. Below Journeyman and at Journeyman a mix yields two potions (the Brewer specialisation makes it three at Journeyman); Master yields three. A potion made entirely from counter-only goods yields one regardless of rank. Potent normally adds 25% magnitude, or duration where magnitude does not apply; Master Alchemist raises that to 40%. Base Potent odds: Expert 10%, Master 20%, plus ingredient, specialization and town bonuses. Cure Disease and Cure Poison cannot become Potent. Consult Crafting and Professions.

## Soul gems

Soul Trap rolls capture when an affected creature dies; carry an empty trap. Filling prefers Azura's Star. Binding uses a carried soul, consuming an ordinary gem or emptying the reusable Star. Some souls force powers and drawbacks. See Mages Guild services.

## Common mistakes

- Spending capacity on one effect before comparing alternatives.
- Ignoring a drawback because its point value is negative.
- Mixing without a recipe or expecting guild mixing to earn profession brewing rewards.

## Next

- Mages Guild services

- Archery and magic

docs.title: Magic item economy
docs.summary: What the item maker's budget and bill are, what soul gems and repairs cost, and when enchanting pays.
headings: Gates, refusals and the online discount
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - An item's enchantment budget is base power + floor(base power × material multiplier); the maker's points and its gold bill are two different sums.
> - Side effects are free in gold and their negative cost buys budget, so a drawback makes an item stronger at the same price rather than cheaper.
> - The maker refuses Aetheric and Gilded pieces, and refuses an already-enchanted item except crafted jewellery that carries its own points.
> - Soul Trap fills Azura's Star first, then an ordinary soul trap; binding a soul spends it (the Star is reused, a gem is consumed).
> - Repairs cost a third of Daggerfall's price; Identify is (25 × value) >> 8 and is free during the Witches Festival.

## The maker's two sums

The item maker at a guild or temple hall spends an item's enchantment points and charges gold. The two arithmetic walks are different and easy to confuse.

| Sum | What it adds | Forced enchantments | Scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Points (capacity used) | Powers and side effects | Excluded | Raw points |
| Gold (the bill) | Powers only | Included | Points × 10 |

A side effect has a negative enchantment cost, so adding it lowers the points used and therefore frees capacity. It contributes nothing to the gold bill, so the freed capacity costs nothing. A forced enchantment — one that a chosen effect drags in, marked by a non-zero parent — is the opposite: it costs gold but no points. That is why drawbacks are worth taking deliberately and forced effects deserve a look before you pay.

## Capacity from the item

capacity = base power + floor(base power × material multiplier); the base power comes from the item's template. The multiplier is negative for iron and rises with the metal:

| Material | Weapons | Armour |
|---|---:|---:|
| Iron | −0.25 | −0.25 |
| Steel | 0 | 0 |
| Leather / chain | — | 0 |
| Silver | +0.75 | +0.75 |
| Elven | +0.25 | +0.25 |
| Dwarven | +0.50 | +0.50 |
| Mithril | +0.25 | +0.25 |
| Adamantium | +0.75 | +0.75 |
| Ebony | +1.00 | +1.00 |
| Orcish | +1.50 | +1.50 |
| Daedric | +2.00 | +2.00 |

Unknown materials fall through to the steel/leather base, so an item with no recognised metal still gets its template's base points. Jewellery generally takes its template's base untouched; a crafted piece of jewellery can also carry its recipe's own points.

## The catalogue: 15 powers and 9 drawbacks

| Powers | Drawbacks |
|---|---|
| Absorbs Spells; Cast When Held; Cast When Strikes; Cast When Used; Enhances Skill; Extra Spell Pts; Feather Weight; Good Rep With; Improves Talents; Increased Weight Allowance; Potent Vs; Regens Health; Repairs Objects; Strengthens Armor; Vampiric Effect | Bad Reactions From; Bad Rep With; Extra Weight; Health Leech; Item Deteriorates; Low Damage Vs; Soul Bound; User Takes Damage; Weakens Armor |

Some entries key a setting. Feather Weight costs 100 points. Extra Spell Pts costs 500 during Winter (200 in some moon conditions; 700–1,000 near a foe group). Item Deteriorates is −3,000 all the time, −1,500 in sunlight or −500 in holy places. Soul Bound has a long per-soul cost row, because the bound soul's identity decides it.

> [!example] Worked capacity and bill
> Feather Weight (100) plus Extra Spell Pts during Winter (500) uses 600 points and costs 6,000 gold. Adding Item Deteriorates in holy places (−500) leaves 100 points used and the bill at 6,000 gold. You accept the item wearing out in temples.

## Gates, refusals and the online discount

The guild service table opens Make Magic Items at Mages Guild rank 5; the maker is a guild or temple service, not a station. The purchase ladder checks the item first, then that something has been prepared, then the gold — so a player who can afford neither hears about gold — then the item's limit.

- At most ten enchantments by the picker guard, and the application truncates in a way that can keep eleven rows; do not plan on eleven.
- Aetheric and Gilded pieces are refused by the port (they carry no ordinary DFU enchantment).
- An already-enchanted item is refused except a crafted piece of jewellery, whose existing enchantments occupy its own points and cannot be removed.
- Online, Enchanting's rank discount is 10% at Journeyman and 20% at Master, and the Efficient specialisation adds five percentage points; the final charge rounds up. The discount is on the gold, not on points.

## Soul gems and Azura's Star

Soul Trap is a Mysticism effect with chance components 40–68 and duration 60–68. The trap effect attaches to the target; when it dies, a re-roll decides capture, and the soul goes to the caster who trapped it, not to whoever lands the killing blow. You need a carried trap.

Filling prefers Azura's Star, the reusable artifact amulet, before any ordinary soul trap; with azurasStarOnly it is the only candidate. Binding a soul to an item spends it: the first ordinary trap holding that soul is removed, and only if none matches is the Star emptied and kept. A filled trap's name shows the soul in brackets. The maker's Soul Bound drawbacks are the binding destination's costs; the trapped soul's identity also decides any forced powers.

Soul value is a property of the monster's row (soulPts), so a Giant's soul is worth far more than a Rat's — but the binding cost, not the soul's point value, is the item-maker side effect you accept.

## Repairs and Identify

Repair is free at full condition. Daggerfall's formula charges ten percent of the item's base value, through the shop's quality and regional adjustment and any guild discount. Online, Roleplay & Realism's condition-based pricing replaces that tenth with a share of the missing condition (0.6, or 0.9 under Instant Repairs), and the port then applies × 1/3 everywhere, floored at 1 gold. The price does not otherwise rise with how damaged the item is; only the time does: 1,000 condition points per game day, floored at one full day. Magic items need the Allow Magic Repairs setting, which is forced on online.

Identify: an unenchanted item is always identified; only enchanted items carry the flag. Shop Identify costs (25 × base value) >> 8, free during the Witches Festival, with guild discounts after the shift. The Identify spell rolls per item against its own chance and charges magicka once, so the service is for gold and the spell is for a caster with the school.

> [!warning] The maker is not a repair shop
> Repair, Identify, Reforge and Temper are separate services with their own rules. The item maker's points cannot be spent on repairs, and a reforge does not refund enchantment capacity.

## When it is worth it

- A high-material item. Daedric, orcish, ebony and adamantium pieces multiply their base points; an iron piece loses a quarter before you start. Enchant the best legal item, not the cheapest one.
- Cheap powers first. Feather Weight, Increased Weight Allowance and Enhances Skill are affordable capacity; a bound-soul power is a late purchase.
- Drawbacks you will not feel. Item Deteriorates in holy places costs 500 points of capacity for a condition you can plan around; a drawback that fires in every fight is a different bargain.
- Permanent gear over disposable gear. The bill is per item; a piece you will replace next level is a poor buy.
- Repair before replace. A third of Daggerfall's repair price is usually less than a new piece, and magic items are repairable online.
- Identify before selling. An unidentified enchanted item's value is not the shop's offer until you know what it is.
- Azura's Star. If you have it, ordinary soul traps are a backup; if you do not, budget gems as a consumable.

The points-and-gold guide is Enchanting, spellmaking and potions; the spell side is Spellmaking maths.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a drawback as a discount on the bill. It buys points, not gold.
- Buying the discount first. The maker checks gold before the item's power limit.
- Enchanting an Aetheric or Gilded piece. Both are refused.
- Expecting a bound soul to be free. It costs points and the binding consumes the trap.
- Repairing to save a cheap item. The floor is 1 gold, but the trip and time are real costs.

## Next

- Spellmaking maths
- Salvage and repair

docs.title: Spellmaking maths
docs.summary: How a made spell is priced, cast and why it fails, with worked examples and the online skill rule.
headings: Where the maker is, and the purchase ladder
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A made spell holds up to three effects; each is priced from its duration, chance and magnitude components, then the whole sum is multiplied by the target type.
> - Your school skill lowers the spell-point cost; online above 100 the cost keeps falling by 100 / skill and never reaches zero.
> - Every cast costs at least 5 spell points, and a spell flagged minimum-cost costs exactly 5 however expensive its effects are.
> - The maker charges gold to buy the spell and shows the spell points to cast it; the editor's per-effect label shows neither the target multiplier nor the floor.
> - Range is CasterOnly, ByTouch (3.0 m), single target, area around caster or area at range (4.0 m explosion); a ranged missile flies at 25 units/s for up to 8 s.

## The two prices

A made spell has two different prices, and mixing them up is the usual mistake.

- Gold is what the maker charges to inscribe the spell. It is the same component sum as the cast price, before the school-skill term.
- Spell points are what a cast costs. They are the per-effect gold priced again through your magic-school skill, summed, multiplied by the target type, then floored.

The spell-point pool itself is floor(Intelligence × your class's spell-point multiplier). The multiplier is a creation choice (Increased Magery raises it); Intelligence raises the pool but does not directly cheapen a spell.

## One effect's cost

For each supported component of an effect:

component gold = trunc(offset + A × starting + B × trunc(increase / perLevel))

The coefficients A, B and offset, and which of duration, chance and magnitude an effect supports, come from the effect's row in EFFECTCOSTTABLE. Some examples:

| Effect | Components | Cost row (A, B) |
|---|---|---|
| Damage Health | magnitude | 20, 28 |
| Heal Health | magnitude | 20, 28 |
| Heal Fatigue | magnitude | 8, 28 |
| Continuous Damage Health | duration, magnitude | 28,8 and 40,28 |
| Paralyze | duration, chance | 28,100 each |
| Soul Trap | duration, chance | 60,68 and 40,68 |
| Shield | duration, magnitude | 28,8 and 80,60 |
| Teleport, Morph Self | none — the fudge 60, 100, offset 160 | |

Magnitude uses the averaged spinner pair: base = trunc((baseMin + baseMax) / 2) and plus = trunc((plusMin + plusMax) / 2). The per-level spinner divides the "increase" part, so level scaling is charged in steps rather than smoothly.

Then the effect's spell points are trunc(gold × (110 − school skill) / 400). Online, once the school is past 100, the term becomes trunc(gold × 10 × 100 / (skill × 400)) — at 200 the spell costs half its at-100 price, never nothing. Offline and to 100, the classic term stands.

The maker's spinner ranges: duration base and modifier 1–60, per level 1–20; chance base and modifier 1–100, per level 1–20; magnitude base low/high 1–100 and level bases 1–100, per level 1–20. A fresh effect starts every spinner at 1.

## Target, area and range

| Target type | Multiplier | What it means |
|---|---:|---|
| CasterOnly | ×1.0 | The caster |
| ByTouch | ×1.0 | A target within 3.0 m |
| SingleTargetAtRange | ×1.5 | One target at range |
| AreaAroundCaster | ×2.0 | A 4.0 m explosion centred on you |
| AreaAtRange | ×2.5 | A 4.0 m explosion at the target |

Sum the effects, multiply both the gold and the spell-point totals by the target multiplier, truncate each. Then apply the floor: no cast under 5 spell points. A spell record flagged minimumCastingCost (vampire clan spells, the lycanthrope morph) costs exactly 5, even if its effects price higher.

Only target and element combinations that every effect allows are offered: targets are intersected and elements are unioned, and Magic is always allowed. An effect that can only target the self forces the self target.

## What a cast does

The spell leaves your hands 0.2 s after the cast starts and the next cast waits 0.7 s from that start; both scale with cast rate. Cast rate is 1 at Speed 50, +25% at Speed 100, −25% at Speed 0, plus cast-speed gear, clamped 0.5–2.

A ranged spell's missile flies at 25 units/s and lives at most 8 s, so movement can make it miss. Whether an effect lands is a saving throw weighing the target's resistances, tolerances and floor(Willpower / 10) magic resist. Magnitude is base + plus × floor(caster level / perLevel).

## Worked examples

A ranged fire bolt. Damage Health, magnitude base 10 (low and high both 10), level part 1, target SingleTargetAtRange. Component = 20 × 10 + 28 × 1 = 228 gold. At Destruction 50 the effect's spell points are trunc(228 × 60 / 400) = 34; ×1.5 = 51 spell points, gold 342. At Destruction 100: trunc(228 × 10 / 400) = 5; ×1.5 = 7 → 7 spell points. At Destruction 150 online: trunc(228 × 10 × 100 / (150 × 400)) = 3; ×1.5 = 4 → floored to 5.

A cheap self heal. Heal Fatigue, magnitude 20, target CasterOnly. Component = 8 × 20 + 28 × 1 = 188 gold. At Restoration 50: trunc(188 × 60 / 400) = 28 → 28 spell points; at Restoration 100: trunc(188 × 10 / 400) = 4 → floored to 5.

These are illustrative builds using the source's rows, not fixed recipes.

## Where the maker is, and the purchase ladder

Making spells is a guild service: Mages Guild members can open Make Spells, and the service tables gate it by membership. Carrying a spellbook item is the first check. The purchase ladder then runs in this order: a spellbook is held, at least one effect is chosen, the gold (coins plus letters of credit) covers the price, and a name is entered. The name is checked last, so an unnamed spell with no gold complains about gold first.

A bought spell is pushed straight onto the spellbook and the maker resets for the next one. The maker's live totals call the same calculateCastCost as the cast, so the gold and spell-point figures it shows are the real ones — except the per-effect editor label, which deliberately omits the target multiplier and the five-point floor.

## Failure modes

- No spellbook. Refused before anything else (record 1703).
- No effect. Refused; an empty spell is never bought.
- No gold. Checked before the item's limits; the maker tells you it is gold, not capacity.
- No name. Checked last.
- Too many effects. The record holds three; a fourth is not carried into the built spell.
- A target no effect allows. The maker restricts the buttons rather than letting you buy an impossible spell.
- Spell Absorption over 50. A made Spell Absorption effect is capped at a 50% base chance.
- Expecting the editor label to match the bill. The single-effect label has no target multiplier and no floor.
- A spell you cannot cast. The floor is 5, but a costly spell can still exceed your pool; the spell points shown are the real cast price.

## Item maker versus spell maker

The spell maker creates spells: gold to inscribe, spell points to cast. The item maker spends an item's enchantment points and charges gold per power point; it does not use your school skills or spell points. See Magic item economy and the overview of both services in Enchanting, spellmaking and potions.

## Common mistakes

- Pricing an area spell as a single-target one. The multiplier applies to the whole sum, both gold and spell points.
- Buying a spell your pool cannot cast. The purchase does not check your maximum spell points.
- Assuming skill 110 makes spells free. Online, past 100 the price falls but never below the 5-point floor.
- Ignoring cast rate. Speed and cast-speed gear change how often the spell leaves your hands, not its price.
- Forgetting the spellbook. The maker will not open the purchase without it.

## Next

- Archery and magic
- Magic item economy

docs.title: Salvage and repair
docs.summary: Welkynd Shards from salvage, repair costs, and resale value.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Salvage eligible found Magic, Rare and Legendary gear for bound Welkynd Shards.
> - Common gear, crafted gear and most special items cannot be salvaged.
> - Online repairs use the item's missing condition in the price calculation, then apply the repair service's one-third scale.
> - A found item's worn condition sets its resale mark; repair does not erase that mark.

## Salvaging gear

Use Salvage on an eligible found item to break it into Welkynd Shards. The shard amount depends on the item's tier:

| Found item | Shards |
|---|---:|
| Magic | 1 |
| Rare | 3 |
| Legendary | 8 |
| Exalted Legendary | 15 |

Salvage refuses Common items, Daggerfall's own ungraded magic items, crafted items, Aetheric and Gilded pieces,
Artifacts, quest items, bound items, worn or locked items, and gear with a gem still set. Remove or extract a gem before
you try. Shards are bound: they stack, but cannot be sold, traded, dropped or listed. Shops exchange 5 shards for a
Portal Stone.

## Repairing gear

Repair a damaged item at a smith or guild service. Online, Roleplay & Realism: Items' condition-price rules are held
whole at their shipped defaults. Its repair calculation uses 0.6 times the fraction of condition missing times the
item's base value, with a minimum of 1; the repair service then charges one third of that result, again with a minimum
of 1. A full-condition item is free to repair. The final price can also reflect a guild discount.

If repairs are not instant, the item takes time and must be collected from the smith where you left it. Online allows
magic repairs. Horses and wagons are not repaired at a smith; a Wagon Yard handles wagons.

## Selling found gear

Gear handed to you in a worn state carries a found mark. At an online counter, the marked condition sets its sale
condition even after a smith repairs it. Your own repairs above that mark receive only partial sale credit; wear after
the find still lowers the item's price. An unmarked item, such as crafted gear, sells by its current condition, and a
crafted item's rolled rarity lines do not add to the counter's base piece value.

This makes repairing useful for keeping equipment, but it does not turn a damaged found item into a higher resale
value than its original mark. Compare repair costs with the item's use to you.

## Common mistakes

- Trying to salvage gear from a shop or a crafting bench. Salvage is for eligible found gear.
- Leaving a gem set. A set gem blocks salvage; unset or extract it first.
- Repairing only to raise a sale price. A found item's original condition mark still governs the counter price.

## Next

- Sockets and reforging
- Loot rarity

docs.title: Craft specialisations
docs.summary: The two-craft limit past rank 50, and profession specialisations.
headings: Choose for the work you do
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - You may raise every gathering track, but only 2 craft tracks may rise above Journeyman (rank 50).
> - Each profession track offers a specialisation choice at rank 50 and rank 100.
> - Disciplines that share a craft track also share its choice slots.
> - You can change a choice later for Marks, but the replacement takes time to become active.

## Choose for the work you do

Specialisations focus a profession. Some improve quality or material yields; others open a new kind of work or improve a specific product. The five craft tracks share their choices across eight disciplines, so a choice for Jewelcrafting or Cooking occupies the same track's specialisation slot as its paired discipline.

| Track or discipline | Rank 50 choices | Rank 100 choices |
|---|---|---|
| Mining | Prospector marks nearby veins; Deep Delver improves dungeon mining. | Motherlode Sense reveals daily Motherlodes sooner; Surveyor opens unwitnessed land ores and direct Cut Stone quarrying. |
| Logging | Lumberjack uses fewer chops; Forester improves Heartwood finds. | Charcoal Burner makes more Charcoal; Timberwright makes more planks. |
| Herbalism | Gardener adds a common herb; Botanist extends the steady window. | Seasonal Eye improves off-season gathering; Apothecary's Friend treats herbs as unbruised. |
| Hunting | Tracker marks nearby animals; Tanner improves hide curing. | Trophy Hunter opens later-gated trophy decor; Butcher improves meat yield and keeping quality. |
| Fishing | Angler widens the tug window; Netter adds fish to a school haul. | Deep-Sea improves Pearl and Slaughterfish chances; Pearl Diver improves Pearl chance. |
| Smithing | Weaponsmith or Armoursmith improves that item's quality. | Masterwright improves Masterwork chance; Quartermaster improves ingot and repair-kit yield. |
| Outfitting | Tailor improves clothing quality; Leatherworker improves leather armor quality. | Couturier opens later-gated two-colour dyes; Saddler opens a later-gated wagon upgrade. |
| Building: Carpentry | Bowyer improves bow quality; Joiner reduces furniture plank costs. | Siegewright improves rams and siege work; Master Joiner marks furniture with its maker. |
| Building: Masonry | Quarryman improves Rough Stone cutting; Builder reduces fortification stone needs. | Fortifier can prevent a seat wall from dropping on capture; Sculptor opens stone decor. |
| Provisioning: Alchemy | Brewer increases potion output; Distiller improves potent brews. | Master Alchemist improves potent brews; Transmuter converts metals with Mercury. |
| Provisioning: Cooking | Cook adds a serving; Field Cook saves fuel at your own Campfire. | Chef extends feast duration; Provisioner prevents rations and dishes from spoiling. |
| Enchanting | Efficient reduces costs; Disenchanter increases Arcane Essence yield. | Soulbinder improves points from filled soul gems; Runecaster lets you choose a Masterwork property from a selection. |
| Smithing: Jewelcrafting | Gemcutter improves set-gem enchantment points; Goldsmith lets Silver count as Gold. | Master Jeweller improves jewelry quality; Lapidary can set siege-cracked Gems as any gem. |

For tracks with paired disciplines, these are alternatives on the same track: you choose one specialisation at each rank threshold, not one per discipline. The choices marked as later-gated are not available until their related feature opens. Read the choice card before committing: specialisations are not all improvements to the same kind of work, and some matter only if you use that system.

## The rank-50 ceiling

Journeyman is the key planning point. You can continue raising all gathering tracks, but only 2 craft tracks can cross rank 50. Disciplines that share Smithing, Building or Provisioning do not create extra craft slots. If you reach the ceiling, another craft cannot keep advancing past it until you make room under the limit.

Changing a specialisation costs Marks and has a waiting period; your current choice remains in effect until the change completes. The law sets the cost and delay. See Money and markets for how Marks differ from gold.

## Next

- Crafting
- Owning a ship

docs.title: Owning a ship
docs.summary: Shipyards, hulls, crew, cargo and naval combat, introduced by The Harbormaster's Word.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - The Harbormaster's Word introduces ship ownership at character level 5.
> - Buy a hull at a port's Shipyard; the Rowboat comes as packable parts, while larger ships enter your Fleet as deeds.
> - Hire named crew at the port's Crew Hall and manage your ship from the shipmaster's services.
> - Naval Combat is enabled online, while some encounter and handling preferences remain your own settings.
> - At sea, another captain can wreck and board your ship; a boarded wreck gives up part of its hold as a prize, but a wreck is not a death.

## Start at a port

The shipyard is the place to buy or sell a hull and arrange work on a ship. It offers the Rowboat, Large Boat, Small Ship, Carrack and Large Galley. The Rowboat is sold as parts that stay in your pack until launched in water. The other hulls are sold as deeds and recorded in your Fleet, with a port berth.

Use the shipyard to arrange refits and shipwright work. The Crew Hall is where you recruit named crew for your deck. Review the shipmaster's listed crew and costs before signing on; the source does not define one fixed fee for every recruit.

## Cargo and a working crew

Your ship's hold gives you a place to carry goods at sea. Manage the hold, rigging, hull, guns, provisions and crew as part of your vessel's upkeep. Larger hulls have different crew and equipment needs, so compare the shipyard's specifications with the kind of voyage you plan.

The Harbormaster's Word is the level-5 introduction to the sea and ship ownership. Its quests ask you to sail, load a hold and strike your colors. For paid travel aboard another captain's vessel, see Ships and passage.

## Fighting other captains

Naval Combat is forced on for shared rooms, so the sea you stand is the room's sea. At the helm, look to one side and hold
Attack to aim a broadside, then release to fire. Another captain can do the same to you.

A ship reduced to a wreck is not a death: its captain keeps the hull's hold through the wreck. A wreck that the
other captain boards gives up a prize — about one third of the hold's worth, at most eight of its most valuable
pieces, held by the account service for the boarder to collect. Piracy is a crime, and pirates can board your ship and
fight you on deck.

## Online rules

Naval Combat is a DFO feature enabled for online play. Its encounter-density, boarding and prize choices are separately declared as player settings. Detailed Ships is forced on for shared rooms, so players there share the same ship decks. Ownership of personal ships comes through Come Sail Away, whose possession setting is player-owned online.

## Next

- Ships and passage
- Craft specialisations

The Rowboat is sold as parts that stay in your pack until launched in water. The other hulls are sold as deeds and recorded in your Fleet, with a port berth.

cargo-and-a-working-crew.title: Cargo and a working crew
cargo-and-a-working-crew.excerpt: Your ship's hold gives you a place to carry goods at sea. Manage the hold, rigging, hull, guns, provisions and crew as part of your vessel's upkeep. Larger hulls have different crew and equipment needs, so compare the shipyard's specifications with the kind of voyage you plan.

fighting-other-captains.title: Fighting other captains
fighting-other-captains.excerpt: Naval Combat is forced on for shared rooms, so the sea you stand is the room's sea. At the helm, look to one side and hold Attack to aim a broadside, then release to fire. Another captain can do the same to you.

online-rules.title: Online rules
online-rules.excerpt: Naval Combat is a DFO feature enabled for online play. Its encounter-density, boarding and prize choices are separately declared as player settings. Detailed Ships is forced on for shared rooms, so players there share the same ship decks. Ownership of personal ships comes through Come Sail Away, whose possession setting is player-owned online.

docs.title: Owning a home
docs.summary: Buying a home online, its storage, bed and entry settings.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A registered account can buy an available town building as an online home at its door.
> - Online homes cost 5000 to 250000 gold; the price depends on the building's footprint and town size.
> - A home belongs to your account: every character of yours may use, furnish and sell it.
> - Each character may count up to three homes against its own cap; deleting that character releases the homes it bought.
> - Your home gives you storage, a bed and a door you can enter at any hour. Set entry to Private, Party, Public or Guild; the default is Private.

## Buy a town building

Online homes are bought at a building's front door and recorded by DFO's account service. Price reflects the building's ground footprint and the town's size, then is rounded and kept within the law's minimum and maximum. If the service cannot measure a building's footprint, that building is not offered for sale.

A home belongs to the account that bought it, not to one character. The character who bought it is recorded as the buyer: its three-home cap counts that home, and deleting that character removes the home from the online world. Every other character on the same account may walk in, keep it, furnish it, rent it out and sell it. A deed that a knightly order grants stays its knight's alone.

This is separate from an offline house in your save: offline ownership does not make a building your registered online home, and an online home does not change your offline save.

## Make the home yours

Your online home provides storage and a bed, and its door stays available to you at any hour. Other players' entry depends on the setting you choose:

| Entry setting | Who can enter |
|---|---|
| Private | You alone |
| Party | You and your party |
| Public | Anyone |
| Guild | Members of your character's guild |

New homes start Private. Change the setting when you want to share your home; the public listing identifies an online home and its owner.

> [!online] Online rule
> A home on the online registry controls online ownership and access. The source explicitly keeps an offline house's storage and bed for its owner when that building is separately purchased online by someone else.

## Next

- Banks
- Taverns and rooms

- Safe storage

docs.title: Safe storage
docs.summary: Where to keep gold, loot, materials and cargo, what each place can lose, and which one fits the goods.
headings: Match the storage to the goods
The bank is for money, not goods
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Gold is safest in the bank: an ordinary death takes one tenth of the gold you carry, and banked gold and letters of credit are outside it.
> - A home gives personal storage and a bed; entry defaults to Private.
> - A wagon carries goods but wears with travel; a ship's hold carries cargo at sea.
> - Profession Stores hold materials for crafting and writs; the Materials Bag holds 300 kg.
> - A guild vault is shared storage: 50 slots, plus 50 if the guild holds a hall.

## Match the storage to the goods

| Place | Holds | Cost or limit | What to know |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bank of the Empire | Gold and letters of credit | Any bank counter; letters cost 1% of their value, and the smallest letter is 100 gold | One account across all regions; carried coins weigh, account gold does not |
| Home | Items, a bed, a private cupboard | 5000–250000 gold; three homes per character; entry Private, Party, Public or Guild | The home belongs to the account; it does not hold gold |
| Wagon | Goods, up to its capacity | Small Cart 750 kg, Open Wagon 1,500 kg, Caravan 2,000 kg | An item in your pack; wears with travel; a town warden can move a badly parked team |
| Ship hold | Cargo at sea | Depends on the hull | A wreck is not a death, but a boarded wreck gives up a prize |
| Profession Stores | Materials for crafting, writs and the market | The Stores law's default cap is 5,000 units a material | Separate from your pack; writs spend from Stores |
| Materials Bag | Raw materials | 300 kg | Sold at General Stores; cannot be sold or dropped while it holds materials |
| Guild vault | Shared items | 50 slots, plus 50 with a guild hall | Rank decides deposit or withdraw; an officer's default withdrawal limit is 10 a day |

## What is lost where

| Event | Carried | Bank | Home | Wagon | Ship hold | Stores and bag | Guild vault |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ordinary death | One tenth of carried gold; items kept | Safe | Safe | Safe | Safe | Safe | Safe |
| Revenant kills you | As ordinary, plus the world-respawn check that can take a piece | Safe | Safe | Safe | Safe | Safe | Safe |
| PvP death in the Open Zone | Eligible carried items and cart contents can remain in shared remains | Safe | Safe | Cart contents exposed | Safe | Safe | Safe |
| Ship wrecked and boarded | — | Safe | — | — | About one third of the hold's worth, at most eight pieces, held for the boarder | — | — |

The ordinary death rule is the one to plan around: death takes a tenth of the gold you carry, rounded down, and leaves the bank and letters of credit alone. The Open Zone and the revenant's thief are separate systems with their own rules. See Dying online, The Open Zone and Revenants.

## The bank is for money, not goods

The bank takes gold and letters of credit; it does not store loot. Online, its account is shared across regions, so a deposit in one town is available in another. A letter of credit carries value without weight and can be deposited later, but its issue costs 1% of its value, with a 100-gold minimum. Keep only the traveling cash you are willing to lose. See Banks.

> [!tip] Before you leave town
> Bank the purse, keep a travel allowance, and carry the gear you might use. The death penalty reaches carried gold only, so an empty purse is a cheap insurance policy.

## Homes, wagons and ships

A home is long-term storage with a bed and a door open at any hour. It belongs to your account, not one character, and each character may count three homes against its cap. The source does not state a single storage capacity for a home; the storage is the home's own. Entry settings decide who can follow you in, and Private is the default. See Owning a home.

A wagon is a pack item you deploy to carry goods, from a 750 kg Small Cart to a 2,000 kg Caravan. It is not a safe: it wears with road and load, and a town's wagon warden can relocate a team that blocks a road or overstays its parking allowance, with the wagon and cargo still yours at the relocation point. In the Open Zone, cart contents can be left in shared remains after PvP death. See Wagons and hauling.

A ship's hold carries cargo at sea. A ship reduced to a wreck is not a death and its captain keeps the hold through the wreck, but a wreck another captain boards gives up about one third of the hold's worth, at most eight of its most valuable pieces, held by the account service for the boarder. See Owning a ship.

## Materials and the guild vault

Profession Stores are the right place for materials. Crafting draws from them, court writs spend from them and the market can list from them, all without adding pack weight. The Materials Bag is the field option: 300 kg of raw materials carried separately from normal encumbrance. See Professions, Gathering and Crafting.

A guild vault is shared storage with two limits: the shelves and your own permission. The guild gets 50 slots, plus 50 more while it holds a hall. Rank sets the default permission: a recruit and member may deposit, an officer may withdraw up to 10 items a day by default, and the guildmaster withdraws without limit; the guildmaster can grant any member a different level and limit. Before depositing anything valuable, read the current guild screen and confirm who can withdraw. See Player guilds.

## A storage routine that works

1. Bank the purse before every trip and keep only the cash you need.
2. Put materials in Stores, not in the pack, as soon as you are done gathering.
3. Carry loot, not cargo: a wagon on a dungeon trip is a liability more than a safe.
4. Use the home for keepsakes and spare gear, not as a bank for gold.
5. Treat the guild vault as shared: deposit only what you can afford to lose if permissions change.

## Common mistakes

- Carrying the whole purse into a dungeon. One death takes a tenth of it; the bank takes nothing.
- Treating the home as a bank. Gold sits in the purse or the bank, not in the home; a home's storage is for items.
- Overloading a wagon and calling it safe. Travel wear and parking rules apply, and Open Zone death can expose cart contents.
- Depositing valuables in a guild vault without checking permissions. An officer's default withdrawal limit still lets an officer take some; the guildmaster's word sets the rest.
- Using the Materials Bag as general storage. It holds raw materials and cannot be sold or dropped while it holds them.

## Next

- Banks
- Owning a home

docs.title: Elites and champions
docs.summary: Stronger foes with halos and traits, and when they appear.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - An Elite is one unusually strong enemy. A champion is a different kind of named enemy with a visible trait.
> - Your own elite encounters begin at Renown 5; a new elite must also meet the character-level floor.
> - An Elite Dungeon is a place with several elite foes. Do not confuse its dungeon tier with an individual foe's promotion.
> - These fights are optional encounters. Leave room to retreat if the foe outmatches you.

## Two kinds of special foe

An Elite has a larger sprite and a pulsing blue outline. Its health and attacks are far stronger than those of its ordinary kind, and it has a separate loot roll. A champion instead has a name and one trait, such as Fiery, Swift or Vampiric. Both can appear in online play; the game treats them as separate promotions.

| What you see | What it means |
|---|---|
| Elite name and blue glow | A foe promoted by Elite Foes; it hits harder and can take much more damage. |
| A named foe and a trait | A champion promotion; the trait gives that foe its special behavior. |
| Elite Dungeon | A dungeon tier that selects several eligible foes as elites. It is a property of the dungeon as well as the enemies inside. |

## When they appear

In the open world, an eligible enemy can be promoted when it is created. Your own open-world and searchable elite rolls wait until Renown 5. The new foe must be at least character level 3. Ordinary dungeons can have no elite or one; an Elite Dungeon selects three or four eligible foes from its layout. A shared dungeon uses the same selection for everyone who enters it.

Champions have their own promotion and trait rules. They are also limited to eligible foes of character level 3 or higher. An elite is not also a champion.

> [!online] Online rule
> Elite Foes, Champions and the loot-rarity system are live in online play under DFO's shared-world settings. Some shared dungeon selections are made from the dungeon layout, while an open-world foe's owner carries its promotion to other players.

## Before you engage

Treat the name and glow as a warning, not as a promise that the reward will make the fight worthwhile for your character. Check your health, supplies and escape route first. Party members can help, but a group fight also changes enemy strength; see Meeting other players.

## Common mistakes

- Treating “Elite Dungeon” as a foe name. The tier describes the dungeon; an Elite is an individual enemy.
- Assuming all nearby foes share one promotion. Each eligible foe is selected separately, and champions and elites are distinct.
- Using a classic or single-player rule as the online rule. Online promotion and shared-room selection are controlled by DFO's own systems.

## Next

- The Arena
- Spawned and Elite dungeons

docs.title: The Arena
docs.summary: Bouts, ladders and rated play, introduced by The Herald's Call.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - The Herald's Call introduces the Arena at character level 6.
> - The Arena has its own rules and referee. Its bouts are separate from ordinary world combat and duels.
> - The ladder is a sequence of bouts against listed opponents. Rated play uses an account rating and seasons.
> - Look at the Arena window before queueing so you know whether you are entering a ladder, exhibition or player bout.

## What the Arena offers

The Arena is a dedicated online match system. It includes a ladder of AI opponents, rated matchmaking and bouts that players can arrange or watch. The Arena window presents its own pages and bout cards. Its rules are handled by the relay, not by ordinary damage between players in the shared world.

The ladder and rated matchmaking are different activities. The ladder advances through its configured opponents; rated matches pair players and update their ratings. Exhibition and private sessions provide other ways to stage or watch bouts. The season clock groups ratings and rewards into fixed eight-week periods.

## Start with the introduction

1. Reach character level 6 and receive The Herald's Call.
2. Follow the quest to the Arena and read the available Arena window pages.
3. Choose a ladder bout or a player match that fits what you want to do. Check whether the option is rated before you enter.

An account is needed for the persistent rated ladder. A rating begins at 1,000; a result moves both ratings according to the rating law, within its 100–4,000 bounds. Repeated matches against the same opponent have a daily and season count limit for rating purposes. After that, a bout may still happen but no longer counts as rated progress.

> [!online] Online rule
> Arena bouts are DFO Online systems. The relay creates and judges their match state; the familiar world combat formulas do not describe a rated Arena hit.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming world combat applies unchanged. The Arena uses a separate referee and match rules.
- Treating every bout as rated. Check its label and the pair's remaining counted matches.
- Confusing the ladder with a season rating. The ladder is a bout sequence; rated matchmaking changes your rating.

## Next

- Arena seasons
- Town raids

docs.title: Town raids
docs.summary: Defending towns from raiders, introduced by The Bay's Troubles.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - The Bay's Troubles introduces town raids at character level 6.
> - A raid is a shared event in a town. Its target and raider group are set for that event.
> - Fight in the town and remain there near the end if you want your contribution considered for the event result.
> - The second introduction step, The Kneeling Dead, waits until Renown 10.

## How a raid works

Raiders attack a selected town during a timed window. The raid targets 15–25 kills, and the event can begin at different points in the shared game day. Its duration is two game hours. Treat the event clock as the authority for whether a raid is active; the town's local time alone does not tell you its full state.

The relay keeps the raid's shared record even if players leave and return. To qualify for the cleanse receipt, you need to strike a raider and be present in town at the event's end. One account can claim one receipt for a given raid. Rewards use the shared combat Marks ceiling, so a receipt does not guarantee that you can collect more Marks that day.

## Join and contribute

1. Check the shared event information for the target town and active raid.
2. Travel to that town and fight its raiders. Party members can help, but the relay tracks participation by account.
3. Be in the town when the raid reaches its target and resolves.
4. Check your account's event receipt and Marks balance afterward.

Raids are not a private dungeon instance. They take place in the shared town cell, and the event record continues across player departures.

> [!online] Online rule
> Raiding Parties is forced on for the shared online world. The raid's kill ledger and reward receipt are relay/account-service records; local mod settings do not decide the shared event.

## Common mistakes

- Arriving after the event ends. A reward requires presence at the cleanse as well as a recorded strike.
- Assuming the raid starts at one fixed game hour. Its start varies within the scheduled day; check the live event information.
- Mixing up the two quest gates. The first Bay's Troubles step opens at level 6; its second step waits for Renown 10.

## Next

- World events and their clock
- Meeting other players

docs.title: World events and their clock
docs.summary: Raids, Motherlodes, Dagon's Breaches and the sea serpent: when and where they happen.
headings: Read the clock before you travel
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - World events follow shared schedules. Use the event display and map before travelling; event clocks can differ from UTC account limits.
> - Town raids last two game hours and can begin at different times in a game day.
> - Three Motherlodes are scheduled each UTC day, each with an open window.
> - Dagon's Breach and the sea serpent have their own phases; their detailed guides explain what to do at each one.

## Read the clock before you travel

DFO Online uses more than one clock. A game day has 1,440 classic minutes; some events schedule against that clock. Account rewards and daily limits can instead reset on UTC. A world event being “daily” therefore does not mean it resets at your local midnight.

| Event | What to expect | Clock to follow |
|---|---|---|
| Town raid | A selected town is attacked for a two-game-hour window. Its start varies within the game day. | Shared game-day event information |
| Motherlode | Three world lodes are scheduled per UTC day. Each has a two-hour open window and a warning before it opens. | UTC schedule and its live warning |
| Dagon's Breach | A daily sequence of omen, rise, opening, seal and Wrath phases. | Shared game-day clock; see Dagon's Breach |
| Sea serpent | A scheduled appearance with omen, rise, seal and sound phases on alternating game days. | Serpent event clock; see The sea serpent |
| Starfall | Several falling stars during a night associated with the seasonal calendar. | Starfall omen and gather window; see Festivals and Starfall |

Motherlodes are shared resource events rather than a personal harvest timer. Their warnings and placement tell you when and where to travel. The sources do not establish a fixed schedule time for each day's lode, so use the live warning instead of planning around an assumed hour.

> [!online] Online rule
> Event schedules are port and shared-world laws. Online mod settings and the server-side receipt rules determine the shared result; an offline calendar or a personal UTC offset cannot replace the event's live phase.

## Plan a short visit

1. Check whether the event is active, announced or still upcoming.
2. Confirm its destination and phase before beginning a long trip.
3. Leave time for the event window, the fight or interaction, and the return trip.
4. Check the account receipt after an event. Daily caps can apply across several event types.

For tactics and rewards, continue to Town raids, Festivals and Starfall, or the event page that matches your goal. This page is only the clock map.

## Common mistakes

- Treating every daily rule as a UTC reset. Some schedules use game time; account caps use service boundaries.
- Travelling on an old schedule. Check the current event phase and target before setting out.
- Assuming every event has a fixed hour. Some laws define a window or warning but not one published start time per event.

## Next

- Catching up in short sessions
- Town raids

docs.title: Festivals and Starfall
docs.summary: Seasonal events, Soul Cakes and falling stars.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Festival dates come from the event calendar and can change. Check the current season in the game.
> - The Witches' Festival enables Soul Cake finds and the related Starfall night.
> - Starfall uses an omen, a brief gather window and three falling stars per night.
> - Account-side find and reward limits apply; do not mistake an event window for a daily personal allowance.

## Seasonal events

The festival calendar determines which seasonal activity is available. The Witches' Festival is the festival tied to Soul Cakes and Starfall. Its questline, The Thirteenth of Frostfall, opens at character level 6 for a registered account while the festival is staged. The event's configuration supplies the current dates, so an older date list is not a reliable standing schedule.

Soul Cakes are event finds. The account service enforces a daily ceiling of 120 cakes and a separate ceiling of 1,500 find requests. Night finds are worth more under the festival law. Those are account limits, not promises that every search will find a cake.

## Follow a Starfall

Starfall's omen tells you a fall is approaching. There are three stars in a Starfall night. A fall has a short gather period, so watch the event indication and act promptly rather than relying on a remembered location or a fixed local hour. The heart star is tied to the Witches' Festival calendar.

1. Check that the festival and Starfall are active.
2. Read the omen and follow the live event indication.
3. Gather during the marked window.
4. Check the account receipt and your daily Starfall claims afterward.

Starfall claims are limited to nine stars per account per UTC day, and Starfall rewards share the daily combat Marks ceiling with other combat events. For event timing across the wider world, see World events and their clock.

> [!online] Online rule
> Festival dates, finds and Starfall claims are controlled by DFO's event and account-service laws. The event's configured calendar and the account receipt are authoritative.

## Common mistakes

- Using last year's dates. The event calendar is configuration data, not a permanent date rule.
- Confusing attempts with rewards. The find-request limit and Soul Cake cap count different things.
- Expecting Starfall to stay open. Each star has a short gather window; follow its omen and live phase.

## Next

- World events and their clock
- The sea serpent

docs.title: Spawned and Elite dungeons
docs.summary: Dungeons that appear in the wilds, their tiers and their loot.
headings: What the label does not tell you
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A spawned dungeon is a temporary dungeon entrance that can appear in the wilderness.
> - Its online label can be Regular Dungeon, Elite Dungeon or Abyss Dungeon.
> - Elite and Abyss are different dungeon tiers; individual Elite foes are a separate system.
> - Check the tier before entering. Shared dungeon layouts and enemy selections are consistent for the players who enter.

## Find a spawned dungeon

The world can create a dungeon entrance in the wild. The spawn system has separate normal and elite rolls; together, they allow a dungeon to appear through either path. A location needs space around it, and a cleared location eventually expires before it can return. The game controls those timers, so do not expect a cleared entrance to remain available indefinitely.

Use the dungeon's online tier label to understand which kind of instance you are approaching. The online dungeon-tier system gives an Abyss Dungeon priority over the Elite Dungeon label when both flags apply.

| Tier shown | How to read it |
|---|---|
| Regular Dungeon | A standard online spawned dungeon. |
| Elite Dungeon | A dungeon tier with multiple selected elite foes and a longer respawn delay. |
| Abyss Dungeon | The player-facing name for a separate shared high-end dungeon system. Its entry and mechanics are covered later in Abyss Dungeons. |

## What the label does not tell you

An Elite Dungeon is not the same thing as a dungeon containing a single Elite foe. Elite Foes promotes individual enemies. The two systems do combine their scaling: an Elite foe in an Elite Dungeon has seven times its ordinary health and four times its ordinary damage. Use the in-game tier and enemy presentation rather than calculating the multipliers yourself.

The Wrothgarian Wild Zone also has its own enemy and dungeon rules. It is a later area; this page does not treat its special scaling as the ordinary dungeon rule.

> [!online] Online rule
> Dungeon tier labels are DFO Online features. The shared dungeon selection comes from the location's layout, while the online dungeon-tier system provides the displayed label. Single-player Daggerfall Unity does not use these tier labels.

## Before you enter

1. Check the dungeon label and your supplies.
2. Make sure your party is ready; dungeon foes and containers are shared-world activity.
3. If the tier is beyond your current comfort, mark the location and return later.

Public dungeon foes and containers respawn on their own timers. Those timers are world behavior, not a personal cooldown. See Elites and champions for individual foe promotions.

## Common mistakes

- Reading “Elite Dungeon” as “every foe is an Elite.” The tier selects a set of foes; it does not rename each one.
- Applying one system's multiplier to another. The source does not establish a simple compounded figure for every path.
- Treating a respawn as your private reset. Foes and containers have separate shared-world timers.

## Next

find-a-spawned-dungeon.excerpt: The world can create a dungeon entrance in the wild. The spawn system has separate normal and elite rolls; together, they allow a dungeon to appear through either path. A location needs space around it, and a cleared location eventually expires before it can return. The game controls those timers, so do not expect a cleared entrance to remain available indefinitely.

The two systems do combine their scaling: an Elite foe in an Elite Dungeon has seven times its ordinary health and four times its ordinary damage. Use the in-game tier and enemy presentation rather than calculating the multipliers yourself.

docs.title: Catching up in short sessions
docs.summary: Daily caps and the event clock, for players with an hour or two.
headings: Know which limits you are seeing
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Check the event display first. World events and account limits use different clocks.
> - Pick one destination and one goal for the session; travel can take longer than the activity.
> - Renown, Marks, festival finds and other account services have separate limits. Reaching one does not mean all play is capped.
> - Save time to bank, repair or return to a safe town before logging out.

## Build a one-hour plan

DFO Online has both live world schedules and account-service limits. A short session works best when you decide which one matters to you before leaving town.

1. Check the clock. Look for an active raid, Motherlode warning, Starfall or another event you want to join.
2. Choose one route. Pick the nearest useful activity or event destination, and account for the journey both ways.
3. Set a personal stopping point. For example, finish one dungeon, complete a profession action, or make one event attempt.
4. Check the account ledger. Confirm receipts and remaining limits rather than repeating an activity whose account cap is already reached.
5. Close safely. Return to town if you need its bank, repair service or other facilities.

## Know which limits you are seeing

Not every number called a cap limits how much you can play. Some limits govern account requests, some limit reward claims, and some describe the schedule or respawn of a world activity.

| Activity | Limit to keep in mind | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Renown | An account-hour XP ceiling | More play is still possible; Renown credit is the limited part. |
| Combat Marks | A shared daily account ceiling | Event rewards can share the same Marks allowance. |
| Starfall | A daily account claim ceiling | Stars have short gather windows as well as a separate account limit. |
| Motherlodes | Three scheduled lodes per UTC day | This is a world schedule; the open window and warning matter. |
| Dungeons | Per-foe and per-container respawn timers | These are shared world timers, not account daily caps. |

The detailed numbers and reset rules are in Caps, timers and resets. Check the live event information for a current schedule; do not use an old festival date or assume that all daily counters reset on one clock.

> [!online] Online rule
> Account caps are enforced by account services. Shared events use their own game-day or UTC schedule. A character's local clock is not a substitute for either.

## Common mistakes

- Planning around a daily number without checking its scope. It may be per account, per character, per opponent pair or per event.
- Treating a world timer like an account limit. A dungeon respawn timer applies to a foe or container, not to your whole character.
- Leaving no time to return. A one-way trip may not fit the session even when the activity does.

## Next

- World events and their clock
- Caps, timers and resets

- Planning a session

docs.title: The sea serpent
docs.summary: Sethrakul and The Old Coil.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - The Old Coil introduces the sea-serpent story at character level 8 for a registered account.
> - The serpent event runs on a shared two-day cycle, with separate omen, rise, seal and sound phases.
> - Travel to the event site during the active window shown by the game.
> - One account receipt is available per serpent; reward limits and event timing are separate.

## Follow the event

The sea serpent, Sethrakul, appears under a shared event law rather than a private quest clock. Its cycle uses a 1,440-minute game day and alternates across two days. The omen comes at hour 2, the serpent rises at hour 5, the storm begins at hour 8 and the sound phase closes the event at hour 10.

The active engagement window begins at the rise and ends when the serpent dives after the sound phase. The storm does not close the waters: ships can still join during the late phase. The omen and the client's sighting/countdown text are the practical cues to use. Check those cues before travelling; the site does not remain open throughout the whole cycle.

## Begin with The Old Coil

At level 8, a registered online account can receive The Old Coil. It introduces the serpent through a three-step questline. Follow the current letter and quest instructions; the event may not be at the needed phase when you first receive a step.

The account service permits one serpent receipt per account for a given appearance. The source does not make that receipt a promise of a fixed item or Marks amount in this page, so check the result in the account ledger after the event.

> [!online] Online rule
> The serpent's phase is shared. Its service receipt is account-scoped, and the event is not an offline Daggerfall Unity encounter.

## Common mistakes

- Travelling at the omen and expecting the fight to be available immediately. The omen precedes the rise.
- Waiting for the site after the sound. The active window ends with the sound phase.
- Confusing the quest with the clock. A quest step can wait for the event even when the quest itself is active.

## Next

- Festivals and Starfall
- Revenants

docs.title: Revenants
docs.summary: Remembered rivals: the Unquiet mark, ranks, escapes, lairs and judgement.
headings: How an enemy becomes a rival
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Revenants are remembered enemies, not a standard enemy respawn. A marked foe must survive a consequential fight.
> - Your revenant encounters begin at Renown 10; eligible foes must also meet the character-level floor.
> - A returning rival can gain rank and adapt to your past encounters. Rank is separate from companion level.
> - After defeating your own revenant, activate its remains and choose Kill or Spare.

## How an enemy becomes a rival

Some eligible elites and champions receive the Unquiet mark. The mark alone is not enough: the foe must survive a fight recorded as consequential before it can become a revenant. Ordinary enemies do not become rivals simply because you defeat them.

Online creation of your revenants waits for Renown 10, and the foe must be at least character level 3. At most three ordinary revenants can be hunting you at once. Dread has separate rules and is not included in that count.

## A rival returns

A revenant can flee when badly hurt, then return later through the shared encounter system. Standard return timing and the encounter chance use your character clock and the revenant's recorded state. The rival can gain ranks from recorded deeds, up to rank V. It may also adapt to your habits. These hunt rules describe a hostile revenant; they do not describe a companion after you spare it.

The source defines the return path, but a guaranteed encounter date is not promised: the return becoming due and the later encounter roll are separate steps. Watch the relevant event or journal information instead of treating the first return window as a fixed appointment.

## Judge the defeated revenant

When your own revenant falls, its remains can be activated for a judgement. Choose Kill to end the rivalry or Spare to attempt recruitment. A successful Spare records a sworn revenant in your retinue, subject to the retinue and active-slot rules on Companions.

> [!online] Online rule
> Revenant creation and return are online systems. The online lane enables their required enemy/loot systems; offline save behavior is not the authority for a shared rival encounter.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming every elite is a revenant. Only some receive the mark, and a consequential fight is needed.
- Treating the return window as a guaranteed spawn. The due time and encounter roll are distinct.
- Using a companion's level to infer a rival's rank. They are separate progressions.

## Next

- Companions
- The sea serpent

docs.title: Companions
docs.summary: Sworn revenants: their own star sky, loyalty, gear, missions and the Dread.
headings: Rank, level and loyalty are different numbers
Stars: the Oath and three aspects
The Dread is a rival's final form
What to do with your first companion
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - A sworn companion begins as a revenant you defeat and Spare; revenants begin at Renown 10.
> - You keep six sworn revenants, but only three companions walk with you, crew included.
> - Its own sky is the Oath and 30 stars in Blade (body), Grave (art) and Road (missions and loyalty).
> - Missions pay coin, materials and gear, but advance only during active online play.

## Open the roster

In the enhanced pause menu open Holdings → Companions. A card offers Call, Send away, Gear, Mission, Stars and Release. A newly spared revenant waits Away when no slot is free. Six sworn is the roster limit; Send away is temporary, Release ends the oath for good.

## Rank, level and loyalty are different numbers

Original rank (I–V) multiplies the body, sets its gear caps and starting star points: health from ×1.25 to ×2.25, ordinary damage from ×1.10 to ×1.50, and 0 to 4 star points. Companion level (1–20) comes from companion XP and only supplies star points. Loyalty (0–100) is how it feels about you.

## Stars: the Oath and three aspects

Its sky is separate from your Firmament: the free Oath and 30 purchasable stars, ten in each aspect, one point each. Points are companion level − 1 plus original rank − 1: 19 at level 20 for rank I, 23 for rank V. Stars must connect back to the Oath; cross-links let you enter a branch sideways. Refunds are free whenever the companion is not abroad.

| Aspect | Branch | What it gives |
|---|---|---|
| Blade | Flesh | +50% health; Deathless −10% damage |
| Blade | Fury | +40% damage; Bloodrage −10% health |
| Blade | both | +40% health, +30% ordinary damage |
| Grave | Power | +40% art strength; Grave Pact −10% health |
| Grave | Rite | 25% shorter art cooldowns |
| Grave | Awakened Art | A fixed art, at 75% of a born art's weight |
| Road | Road | +5 points of mission odds, +40% haul |
| Road | Oath | 50% smaller loyalty losses, 50% shorter rests |

Fortune's Road returns nothing from a hard-won mission; Undying Vigil makes missions 10% longer. Only about a third of revenants are born with an art, which Grave stars strengthen; the rest gain nothing from Grave until Awakened Art.

## Loyalty

Starting loyalty comes from personality, from Honourable at 80 down to Unhinged at 40; the rest sit between. A won fight gives +3 and a character day with you +2; a day away −1, a knockout −8, a repeated sending the same day −10, executing a revenant of its kind in its sight −15, and the first call after a knockout +10.

Devoted (90+) adds 10% ordinary damage, warns you about a wind-up behind you and adds 5 percentage points to mission odds; Loyal is 50–89, Wavering 20–49, Restless below 20. Below 20 it rolls a 15% daily chance to desert, which resting does not prevent; being abroad does. Below 10, a Brutal, Craven or Unhinged companion may become a Betrayer when a hit leaves you below 25% health. A leaver keeps the more valuable half of its pack and given gear, within three items; its XP and stars are lost.

## Equipment, falls and following

An armed kind wears ten given pieces: melee weapon, shield, helm, two pauldrons, cuirass, gauntlets, greaves, boots and one charm. Other kinds get the charm only. Bows, artifacts, Aetheric and Gilded gear, quest and summoned items and broken pieces are refused.

Given gear replaces rolled gear, wears and can break, and adds mission power: 0.05 plus 0.10 to 0.35 by rarity, capped at 2. Rank caps it: Silver and Magic at rank I, Dwarven and Rare at II, Adamantium and Rare at III, Orcish and Legendary at IV, Daedric and Legendary at V.

It follows through doors, catching up when more than 40 m behind or 6 m above or below you. A knockout sends it to rest for 8 character hours, about 40 real minutes online, before Call works again; your death does not kill or release it. In the Open Zone only one stands beside you, and Send away and Mission are blocked; Release returns its things but ends the oath.

## Missions: odds, rewards and risks

Choose Mission, then a province and a venture. A province sets the days and danger: High Rock 1 day at danger I, Black Marsh 4 days at danger V. Plunder leans gold and loot (0.40× gold, 0.35× materials, a piece per road day), Forage materials (0.15× gold, full materials, 20% piece) and Sell-sword coin (full gold, 25% piece).

Online a character day is two real hours, and progress counts only lived time; logging off does not finish a mission. At most two companions are abroad at once.

Odds are 55% + 10 percentage points × (rank + gear power + Road odds − danger) + 5 if Devoted, clamped 30–95%; a bare rank-I companion has 55% in High Rock and the 30% floor in Black Marsh.

The haul scales with your character level at return, the province's days, danger, rank, venture and haul stars. Per piece, Legendary is 0.5% + 0.4% per danger + 0.3% per rank past I, at most about 3.7%. Missions give companion XP only below level 10 and give you no character XP or Renown.

A hard-won result brings half the haul and an 8-hour rest with no loyalty gain; an early recall loses the haul and still costs the rest. There is no mission death or permanent loss, and loyalty is frozen abroad.

## The Dread is a rival's final form

A hostile rank-V revenant with a lair that escapes again can ascend to the Dread — a rival's final form, not a companion promotion. Only one exists; it stays in its lair, does not flee or fester, has ×1.5 its rank's health and two last stands, 40% then 25%.

Kill it for a guaranteed Legendary trophy and a gold hoard at least ×3; Spare it for an ordinary rank-V companion with four starting star points.

## What to do with your first companion

1. Read its rank, personality, loyalty, level and art; without a born art, read the Awakening preview before spending Grave points.
2. Call it and keep it in fights you can manage; a won fight is +3 loyalty, and Devoted is worth having.
3. Spend first points on Blade health, or on Road if you will send it out; refunds are free at your side.
4. Give it spare gear within its rank caps and watch condition.
5. If it falls, wait out the rest; repeated falls mean more health, better gear or easier fights. Do not test it in the Open Zone, and do not send your only fighter away before a session.

## Common mistakes

- Sparing without checking your slots. A companion can be sworn but Away if the three shared slots are full.
- Confusing loyalty, level and rank. Each drives a different part of its strength.
- Assuming every item fits. The rank cap refuses better metal and rarer gear.
- Sending your only fighter away. Missions need hours of active play and give no help while abroad.

## Next

- Revenants
- Player guilds

docs.title: Dagon's Breach
docs.summary: The Breach world boss, its portents and the Warden, introduced by The Burning Doors.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - The Burning Doors introduces Dagon's Breach at character level 10 for a registered account.
> - The shared event runs each two-real-hour game day, with an omen at 17:00 and an entry window from 20:00 to 22:00 on the event clock (two real hours per game day, so the window lasts about ten real minutes; this is not the sky clock you see).
> - A portent changes what happens at the Breach. Check the active omen and current event instructions.
> - The Warden and Breach phases are shared event rules; the questline advances through its witnessed steps.

## Read the Breach's phases

Dagon's Breach uses a 1,440-minute shared game day. The omen begins at 17:00, the gate rises at 19:00, entry opens at 20:00, and the gate seals at 22:00. Wrath follows at the end of the game day. These are game-clock times, not UTC schedule labels.

The event draws one of three portents: The Vanguard, The Sundering or The Captive. A Dire Breach can combine Vanguard and Sundering. Read the current event display to learn which portent is active and what the game expects you to do; do not assume the same encounter is present every time.

## Begin The Burning Doors

At character level 10, a registered account can begin The Burning Doors. Its five steps introduce the Breach story. Some steps wait for a witnessed event action, so progress is tied to the server's record rather than simply entering the quest location. The line leads to later content through The Covens' Hoard and The Weir Road; those later systems are covered in Elite Gates.

An account can claim a gate receipt once for each gate. Combat Marks earned from the event share the daily combat Marks ceiling with other combat events. Check your receipt and Marks ledger after the event.

> [!online] Online rule
> The Breach schedule, gate phases and reward receipts are DFO Online port/account systems. The game day drives the event; the account service records claims.

## Common mistakes

- Arriving during the omen. The gate does not open until 20:00 on the event clock.
- Using UTC to read the event phase. UTC is used for account-day limits; this gate follows the event clock, not UTC or the sky clock.
- Expecting every visit to use the same portent. Read the live event information.

## Next

- World events and their clock
- Elite Gates

docs.title: Player guilds
docs.summary: Joining and founding a guild, ranks, vault and chapters.
headings: Connect a guild to city control
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Player guilds are online account groups, separate from the NPC guilds and orders in town.
> - Joining is by invitation. Founding requires Renown 10 and 10000 gold.
> - Guildmaster, Officer, Member and Recruit are distinct ranks with different permissions.
> - A guild vault stores shared items; permissions and capacity depend on guild state and facilities.

## Join or found a guild

An existing guild invites you to join. If you want to found one, meet the Renown requirement and pay the founding cost. The service allows up to 75 characters in a guild. The Guildmaster and Officers can manage different guild actions; membership rank controls which actions are available.

| Rank | What it means |
|---|---|
| Guildmaster | Leads the guild and holds its highest permissions. |
| Officer | Can perform the officer actions granted by the guild law. |
| Member | A full guild member without officer controls. |
| Recruit | A newly admitted or lower-rank member. |

The exact permission checks belong to the guild service. Before depositing valuable items or Marks, read the current guild screen and confirm who can withdraw or spend them.

## Guild vault and town chapters

The guild vault is the player guild's shared storage. Its capacity and permissions can change with guild facilities. Use the vault law and the guild UI as the authority for what you may deposit or withdraw.

“Chapter” can also mean an NPC guild chapter: a local branch of a Fighters Guild, Mages Guild, temple or order. That is separate from a player guild's ranks and permissions. Joining an NPC chapter does not make you a player-guild officer or grant authority over a town seat. See NPC guilds for those organizations.

## Connect a guild to city control

Player guilds can pledge towns and compete for a Charter through the seat system. That is a separate weekly activity with its own influence, fee and upkeep rules. A guild membership alone does not mean that the guild holds a town. Continue to City control for how pledges and Charters work.

> [!online] Online rule
> Player guilds are backed by DFO's account service. Offline NPC guilds are a different game system; offline membership does not create an online player guild.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing NPC guild membership with a player guild. They have different rosters, services and progression.
- Assuming every guild member can withdraw from the vault. Guild rank and vault permissions govern access.
- Assuming a pledge already means the guild owns a town. A Charter is resolved at the weekly Turning.

## Next

- City control
- NPC guilds
