docs.title: City control
docs.summary: Seats, influence, the weekly Turning, edicts and sieges.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Player guilds compete for a town's seat, its Charter, through influence; membership gives nothing.
> - The week runs Turning to Turning. Pledges lock at the Reckoning (Friday 18:00 UTC); the Turning settles Sunday 18:00 UTC.
> - An account is capped at 2,000 influence per seat per week; a Palace needs 6,000, a Crown 30,000. A held Charter has upkeep and can be challenged by a Right of Siege.

## Which towns have seats

A seat is a town's player-guild Charter. The three Crown seats are Daggerfall, Wayrest and Sentinel; every other location with a Palace in its records is a Palace seat. A town without a Palace has none, and a location is one seat however many Palaces it holds. Crown reach and the Free Lands' Watch bonus boost claims.

## Pledge a town

The week has three parts: Muster, from Sunday's Turning; Reckoning, its last 48 hours; Turning, when everything settles. A Guildmaster or Officer pledges during the Muster: one seat in a region, in up to five regions. Pledges lock at the Reckoning, but influence earned then still counts. A guild that holds a seat is pledged there automatically and cannot pledge to another seat in that region; unpledged work earns nothing. Influence counts for the guild your account is bound to — the first guild one of your characters contributes to that week — and only from a character seven days in the guild.

## Earn influence

| Contribution | Influence | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| The Watch | 1 per tick | Online in the seat town, moving; 60 a UTC day |
| Oblivion Gate | 300 a receipt | 3 claims in the region must agree; 900 an account a week |
| Renown in the region | 1 per 20 XP | 400 an account a week |
| A home in the seat town | 25 a whole day | 5 homes per guild at that seat |
| Seat writ | 1 per Mark of value | Own units count fully; bought units at Tribute's rate |
| Tribute | 1 per 10 Marks | Spent; at most a fifth of the guild's whole week at that seat; Guildmaster only |
| Orc Raid camp | 50 a camp | During its Tide; 5 a day, 250 an account a week |

Each account contributes at most 2,000 influence per seat per week. Ten percent of a guild's influence carries into the next week as Legacy.

## Thresholds, fees and upkeep

| Seat | Claim threshold | Fee | Upkeep a week |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Palace | 6,000 | 8,000 Marks | 2,500 × the server's activity scale |
| Crown | 30,000 | 80,000 Marks | 15,000 × the server's activity scale |

A claim needs the threshold and the fee in the guild's Marks treasury. If the second claimant is within 10% of the first on an unheld seat, neither takes it: the two fight a Tourney.

Holding more than one seat costs more: upkeep rises 25% per extra seat-weight and defence falls 5%, with a Palace weighing 1 and a Crown 3. Standing starts at 50 and caps at 100, and shifts defence. A short Marks balance puts the Charter into Neglect at −10 Standing, and a second short week in a row lapses it.

## What holding a Charter gives

The holder sets a whole-number Tithe once a week: up to 10% at a Palace and 15% at a Crown, a Market Hall raising the cap. It comes from local sales and board fees and goes to the guild's treasury.

The holder sets one Edict a week, paid at the Turning; the same Edict cannot repeat except Market Day, which cuts shop prices 10% for everyone. Members get 10% off at a Palace or 15% at a Crown, and Standing 80 adds 5%.

## Sieges and fortifications

The Turning names a Right of Siege for a held seat. The holder picks the day and start hour, Wednesday to Saturday between 16:00 and 02:00 UTC (default Wednesday 20:00). A Palace battle lasts 30 minutes, a Crown battle 45, a Tourney 20, and rosters close 10 minutes before. A side fields 10 at a Palace or 20 at a Crown, plus up to 2 or 4 Sellswords; a fighter must have been seven days in the guild at the Turning and bound to it in the week that won the Right.

At a Palace the attackers take the Gate, Market and Temple banners, then hold the Throne: 2 of 3 banners opens it, and the Throne must stay uncontested for 120 seconds. A Palace with tier-3 Walls adds a Gatehouse. At a Crown they need 3 of 4 banners, then the Gatehouse, then 180 seconds on the Throne. A Gatehouse must be breached. If time runs out the holder keeps the seat.

A defence adds 15 Standing (10 if the attackers reached the Throne) and 20% defence at the next Turning; a forfeit gives 10 and the same bonus. A capture moves the Charter, drops each fortification one tier and clears the former holder's Legacy.

Fortifications: Walls quicken defender waves; Gatehouse adds 50% gate vitality a tier and needs a Crown or tier-3 Walls; Watchtowers warn at half or a quarter of the defence; Barracks add guards; a Market Hall adds listings and Tithe cap; a Shrine adds gate influence and Standing. A project stands 2, 4 or 7 days after its last material, and seat writs supply it.

> [!example] What a guild does in a week
> A five-member guild targets a Palace. The Officer pledges during the Muster. Through the week they patrol the town for Watch ticks, run one gate and deliver gathered materials to the seat writ. Suppose four accounts finish on 1,500 influence each: that is 6,000, exactly the Palace threshold, and every account is under the cap.
>
> At the Turning the claim succeeds if the treasury can pay the 8,000 Marks fee and the coming week's upkeep. At an activity scale of 1.0 that is 2,500 Marks, so plan for about 10,500 Marks for the first week. A Crown's 30,000 needs about fifteen capped accounts, so Crowns usually belong to large guilds. These figures are an example, not a plan.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing a pledge with a Charter. The claim resolves at the Turning and must meet its tier's threshold and fee.
- Contributing too early. Your character must be seven days in the guild.
- Burning Marks on Tribute first. Tribute is capped at a fifth of the guild's whole week and is spent.
- Assuming a guild can keep a seat without upkeep. Unpaid Charters lapse, and several seats cost more.

## Next

- Player guilds
- The Arena

docs.title: Example build plans
docs.summary: Three example plans, a fighter, a caster hybrid and a thief, with the trade each one makes.
headings: Plan 3 — The thief and utility plan
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - These are three worked examples, not a ranking. There is no best build; each plan pays for its strength somewhere else.
> - Each online level gives 5 attribute points; class difficulty sets skill growth, from ×0.30 to ×3.00.
> - 1–10 is the class's damage skill, a safe routine and legal gear; 10+ is masteries, a specialisation, the Firmament and better loot.
> - Free Firmament refunds end at Renown 10, so experiment before then.

## How to read a plan

These plans follow the game's numbers: the creation rules, the level formula, five mastery slots and the Firmament's caps.

Only class skills move the level sum. Gear and the Firmament carry the caps the attributes cannot reach, so a plan spends its stars on the channels it reads.

Skills start at 28–31 / 18–21 / 13–16 by tier, and Health per level (4–30) sets difficulty and growth.

## Plan 1 — The fighter

The idea. One weapon family, or fists with Gauntlets, plus Critical Strike and Dodging. Stay in the fight; let gear and masteries carry the late game.

Attributes. Speed, then Strength; Luck and Agility next; Endurance after them. Speed sets swing time, Strength adds damage, Luck raises criticals, and Endurance raises the health floor.

Skills. Primary: the weapon skill, Critical Strike, Dodging. Major: Running and support such as Stealth or Medical. Minor: Backstabbing and movement.

The measured example. The Tiger Fist preset is the measured example (HP 30, difficulty floor, ×0.30 growth); it is not a prescription.

Order, 1–10. Use the damage skill in real fights, rest when the 360-minute skill check is due, take quests for private rooms and gear, keep armour legal and bank gold. Master the damage skill at 100.

Order, 10+. Master five skills: two primary, two major, one minor. Critical Strike in the second primary slot for offence, or Dodging for defence. A martial path needs two mastered weapon skills, which may mean a skill swap. Spend Firmament stars on weapon damage to its +30% cap, then on survival. Replace gear from hard content, not the anvil.

What it gives up. Recall, Levitate and Water Breathing (potions instead), ranged answers, social skills; forbidden materials narrow the armour ladder. A pure fighter offers a group little besides damage.

## Plan 2 — The caster hybrid

The idea. One or two spell schools plus a weapon for the moments when spell points run out. Peak power in either half is traded for never being helpless.

Attributes. Intelligence first (spell points are the class multiplier times Intelligence), Willpower next (the defence against hostile spells and poison), then Endurance, then Speed or Agility for the weapon.

Creation. A custom class with a magic school in primary or major starts with the Spellsword's spells. Increased Magery sets the multiplier: ×1.5 costs 4 difficulty points, ×2 costs 8 and ×3 costs 10.

Skills. Primary: Destruction, a weapon, and a defensive school or Dodging. Major: Restoration or Mysticism, Running and one support. Minor: the other schools.

Order, 1–10. Cast the schools you want in real fights, and keep the weapon skill moving. Buy or make spells. Master one school at 100 first; it is the one your damage reads.

Order, 10+. Master a second school: two mastered schools open the arcane paths. A hybrid may hold one arcane and one martial path, but the martial one needs two mastered weapon skills, so plan a swap. In the Firmament, spell damage caps at +30%, spell cost at 25% less, and spell points at +75 raw and +15%; take those, then blows taken, then health. Buy spell and magicka gear from rewards.

What it gives up. Health and armour next to the fighter, and two mastery groups that narrow the skill slots. Half its investment sits in a weapon a pure caster would skip.

## Plan 3 — The thief and utility plan

The idea. Stealth, locks and pockets, with a short blade for fights the plan cannot avoid. It profits from access, not a long fight.

Attributes. Agility and Speed first, Luck next, Personality and Endurance after them. Agility keeps the hit chance usable, Speed the swing, Luck the criticals; Personality helps prices and reactions.

Skills. Primary: Stealth, Lockpicking, Short Blade. Major: Pickpocket, Backstabbing, Dodging or Running. Minor: Streetwise, Mercantile, Medical and movement.

Order, 1–10. Sneak on real approaches; backstab when a foe is facing away (your Backstabbing skill, triple damage on success); pick only locks whose look text supports you; stay out of the watch's way. The Thieves Guild invites after 10 thefts, the Dark Brotherhood after 15 murders; Thievery has the risks.

Order, 10+. Master Stealth first, then Lockpicking or Backstabbing. Cutthroat, Assassin and Shadowdancer each need two mastered weapon skills, so a swap may be the bridge. The Firmament's channel against unaware foes caps at +40%, and evade at 10%. Keep light armour and skill gear.

What it gives up. A straight fight, area damage and staying power. Against a boss, a raid or a Watchful foe it loses its best trick, so it wants a party.

## What all three share

- Levels and checks. Class skills build the level sum: three primaries, the two best majors and the best minor. Each level gives 5 attribute points, and maximum health is floored for your permanent Endurance. Uses are checked after 360 classic minutes; training stops at 50; past 100 only tough foes teach.
- Masteries. Two primary, two major and one minor, chosen at 100 and permanent.
- The Firmament. Two stars per Renown past the first (18 at Renown 10, 98 at 50); craft points come from profession ranks and reach the life ring only. Refunds are free below Renown 10 and cost 10 Marks per star after; a full respec costs 10,000 gold.
- Gear and prices. Crafted gear tops at Masterwork, about one Rare roll; quest cards fit your armour and best weapon (Magic low, Rare higher). A skill swap costs 100,000 gold and a path reset 200,000 per family. Do not rush levels on weak gear; The hero's threat explains why.

## Common mistakes

- Treating an example as the answer. The plans are shapes; the caps and the class you enjoy decide the details.
- Copying an attribute order without its skills. Speed does little for a plan whose damage is a spell.
- Spending a mastery before checking the paths it opens. Masteries cannot be refunded or moved.
- Buying a reset before a skill swap. The swap is cheaper when the class is short a weapon skill.

## Next

- Masteries and specialisations
- The Firmament

- Beginner online builds

docs.title: Elite Gates and the Elite Breach
docs.summary: Follow The Weir Road, carry Weir Keys, and learn how Redoubts fit into the Elite Breach.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Finish The Covens' Hoard before the Weir Road introduction line opens.
> - Weir Keys are inventory items used by the Elite Gate system; keep them available when you approach its service.
> - /breach opens the Elite Breach commands; /breach help lists them.
> - A Redoubt's Marks reward is per Redoubt and per account for an Arena week, not one reward for the whole Breach.

## Follow The Weir Road

The late-game progression is a questline, not a single character-level check. The Weir Road follows The Covens' Hoard and introduces the Elite Gate sequence. The questline table records the line and its step prerequisites; follow the current journal and gate prompts for the step you have reached.

The account service awards Weir Keys for qualifying Dagon's Breach kills and completed Elite Breach runs; the odds and pity rules differ by event. Your account balance appears as one stackable item in your pack. Using a key opens a start window and stakes one key when the service accepts the open, so keep the item in your pack and follow the live prompt.

## The Elite Breach and Redoubts

The Elite Breach is a shared, scheduled challenge built from halls called Redoubts. Its service and client share the gate's current law. Use /breach for the command entry and /breach help for the available commands.

Each Redoubt can pay 20 Marks once per account per Redoubt per Arena week. That receipt also counts toward the shared combat-Marks daily limit. Completing one Redoubt therefore does not by itself spend every reward opportunity in the Breach; the receipt is scoped to that named Redoubt.

The ordinary elite and champion rules are separate from the Breach. Elites begin appearing in your own world at character level 3 and Renown 5; that gate does not unlock the Weir Road or guarantee a Breach entry.

> [!warning] Bring the right expectation
> Redoubt rewards are once per account, Redoubt and Arena week. Weir Key awards have different rules for Breach kills and completed Hours; there is no single drop rate for every event. Check the active service and quest text for current entry details.

## Common mistakes

- Treating level 3 and Renown 5 as the Elite Breach gate confuses ordinary elites with the later Weir Road progression.
- Assuming one Redoubt clears the weekly reward for every Redoubt ignores the per-Redoubt receipt.
- Treating the key's item template as proof of its issuance conditions skips the quest and server service that decide when you receive or spend it.

## Next

- Abyss Dungeons

docs.title: Abyss Dungeons
docs.summary: Find the shared Abyss Dungeon while it is open, and separate its world event from the level-gated questline.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - The Abyss Dungeon is a shared, temporary dungeon that rises in an eligible region when enough accounts are present.
> - Find its entrance before you can enter; the dungeon admits players only during its found phase.
> - An unbeaten dungeon remains for up to 48 hours; after defeat it collapses, then waits through a cooldown.
> - The Hour That Was Not is a separate level-12 questline, not the spawn gate for the world dungeon.

## Find the shared dungeon

The Abyss Dungeon is the player-facing name for the system whose internal source name is Super Dungeon. It is one shared world instance, not a personal dungeon that appears whenever you reach a level. The director checks a regional census, requires at least two accounts, and selects an eligible region with the most players; some regions are excluded.

The first rise is delayed. When the entrance is available, discover it in the world. The server admits players only after the dungeon reaches its found phase, and stops admitting them when it falls or closes. The ocean-hole systems place its entrances on the seafloor, so approach prepared for underwater exploration.

## Watch its window

An unbeaten dungeon lasts 48 hours. Defeating it starts a three-minute collapse, followed by a two-hour cooldown before another can rise. These are shared world-event timers, not personal daily attempts.

The underwater dungeon uses replacement enemies and upgraded loot. Online, the Iliac Puddle and Ocean Holes systems are part of the shared-world rules. The level that opens the separate questline does not change the dungeon's timer.

## The Hour That Was Not

At character level 12, The Hour That Was Not introduces the Abyss Dungeon questline. Keep that introduction distinct from the shared event: the event's own conditions are its census, region selection, spawn phase and discovery state.

## Common mistakes

- Waiting until level 12 to look for the world event confuses its questline with its timed spawn.
- Arriving after the dungeon has fallen or closed does not create a personal instance; wait for the shared event cycle.
- Calling the source's internal name “Super Dungeon” can make event notices harder to recognize; the player-facing name is Abyss Dungeon.

## Next

- Elite Gates and the Elite Breach
- The Eltheric Ocean

docs.title: Masteries and specialisations
docs.summary: Mastering skills at 100, the climb to 200, and the thirty specialisation paths.
headings: The path reset: 200,000 gold per family
What is and is not reversible
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - At skill 100 you may master an eligible class skill if its group has a free slot: 2 primary, 2 major and 1 minor, five in all. A mastery is permanent.
> - A mastered skill can reach 200, at 4×, 8× and 16× the uses a point, worth a quarter point each, with milestone bonuses at 125, 150, 175 and 200.
> - Past 100 a skill learns only from foes tough for it; weak enemies and repetition teach nothing.
> - Two mastered schools or two mastered weapon skills open a specialisation path: one arcane and one martial may be held together. A path reset costs 200,000 gold per family; a class skill swap costs 100,000 gold.

## Mastering a skill

Online, Master Skills is always active. When a primary, major or minor skill reaches 100, the game offers to master it; you can also choose later from the skill screen. Slots are separate by career group: two primary, two major and one minor. Miscellaneous skills can never be mastered and stop at 100.

The choice is permanent: you cannot unmaster a skill, move its slot or refund it. Mastering also lifts Daggerfall's old rule that holds other skills at 95 once a primary skill is mastered, so every skill can reach 100. Only a mastered skill passes it.

## Progress above 100

A mastered skill grows to a hard cap of 200. The climb is slow: 4× the uses a point from 100 to 125, 8× from 125 to 150 and 16× from 150 to 200. Points above 100 count a quarter each in every formula, and milestones add effective points on top: 125 Expert +2, 150 Master +3, 175 Grandmaster +4, 200 Legend +6.

That is 25 points from the climb plus 15 from the milestones, so a sheet showing 200 reads as 140 to the formulas.

Past 100, a use counts only when the foe is tough for that skill. The foe's tier is 5 × its level + 30, measured against the skill's value: below three quarters of the skill nothing counts, from there to the skill's value the weight ramps in, and above it up to one and a half times. At 100 a foe of about level 9 starts to teach and level 14 teaches fully; at 150 those are about level 17 and 24; at 200 about 24 and 34. Running, jumping, swimming and climbing instead count ground actually covered, and repeated use is damped, so nothing trains a mastery AFK.

## Specialisation paths

Mastering two of the six spell schools opens the arcane paths: fifteen, one for each pair of schools. Mastering two of the six weapon skills opens the martial paths: also fifteen, one for each pair. A character may hold one arcane and one martial path at the same time.

Each path gives a passive effect and a signature: an arcane path a signature spell, a martial path a weapon technique that answers on the technique key when the weapon in hand is one of its pair's. You choose once two of its skills are mastered, from the Specialisations guide on the Growth tab, which shows which paths are ready. Like a mastery, the choice is permanent unless you pay for a reset. The design records are bible/06-Systems/Arcane-Specialisations.md and bible/05-Combat/Martial-Specialisations.md.

## The skill swap: 100,000 gold

A class's skill lists are fixed at creation, so a class holding one weapon skill could never master the two a martial path needs. Skill swap gives up one class skill you have not mastered and takes one skill from outside your class in its place. Primary goes to primary, major to major, minor to minor, so the 2/2/1 slots and every mastery already spent stand.

The swap costs 100,000 gold a time. Skill values and your character level do not move: a swap that lowers the class's skill sum leaves the level where it stands, and the class's skills make up the ground before the next level. Online the gold comes from coins, letters of credit and then the Empire's account. The swap is repeatable — the skill you give up is then outside the class — so another paid swap can bring it back.

## The path reset: 200,000 gold per family

A chosen path can be given up for 200,000 gold, once for the arcane family and once for the martial. The reset clears only that path. Your masteries stay, so the guide offers every path those masteries open.

The signature spell stays in your book. Without its path it is the plain spell the spell maker could have made: its path pricing and rider no longer apply. The reset marks that family's choice as asked, so the game does not prompt you to choose back the path you paid to remove.

## What is and is not reversible

| Change | Cost | Reversible? |
|---|---|---|
| Master a skill | Free at 100, one group slot | No |
| Climb past 100 | Uses | Not undone; the points stay |
| Choose a path | Free | Yes, 200,000 gold per family |
| Swap a class skill | 100,000 gold | Yes, by another swap |
| Signature spell after a reset | — | Kept, without path powers |

## Common mistakes

- Expecting a skill at 100 to rise automatically. It must be mastered, with a slot free in its group.
- Spending a slot without checking the paths you want. Masteries cannot be refunded or moved.
- Training past 100 on weak foes. Below the foe tier nothing counts, however long you repeat it.
- Expecting a 200 to act like a 200. Formulas read 140, and the last 50 points cost 16× each.
- Confusing a reset with a mastery refund. A reset clears only the chosen path.
- Swapping a mastered skill. The swap only accepts a class skill you have not mastered.

## Next

- The hero's threat
- The Firmament

docs.title: PvP and duels
docs.summary: Start consensual duels, distinguish Arena ratings, and understand what open PvP puts at risk.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Use another player's Inspect card to challenge them; they must accept.
> - An ordinary duel uses separate vitality and leaves your real health untouched.
> - Arena rated and casual bouts are separate from outdoor challenges.
> - The mountains and the ocean beyond Veilhaven's peace allow open PvP.
> - Open-zone death can cost carried goods and an equipped item, with a two-minute hold before return.

## Challenge another player

Meet the other player outdoors, open their Inspect card and choose Challenge. The other player receives a prompt and can accept or decline. You both need to remain alive, outdoors and near each other while the challenge becomes a bout. The source sets the challenge range to 10 metres.

An acceptance is followed by confirmation from the challenger. If you move away, enter a building or lose the connection during that exchange, do not assume the duel has begun. Wait for the game's countdown and ring rather than attacking on the strength of a chat agreement.

The ring forms around the midpoint between you. Stay inside it while fighting. Yielding, leaving the ring or disappearing from the room can give your opponent the win; reaching the bout's time limit produces a draw. Decline before the start if you do not want to fight. Accepting and then walking away is not the same decision.

## Understand the stakes

An ordinary duel is a refereed contest with its own duel vitality. Damage goes to that separate pool. Your real health is never reduced to make the result happen, and the duel does not heal your real character afterward. A duel loss therefore does not send you through the ordinary death-and-respawn penalty.

The result can count toward your account's duel win/loss record. That record is different from Arena rating. The checked duel source does not set selectable rated and unrated outdoor challenge modes, a gold wager, an item stake or an automatic purse payment to the winner. Do not interpret a recorded loss as an Arena rating loss, or promise another player that the game will enforce a private wager.

The consent applies to the pair in that bout. It does not authorize bystanders to damage either fighter in ordinary co-op. Elsewhere in normal shared play, player melee, arrows, spells and techniques do not become unrestricted attacks merely because players stand near each other.

## Separate Arena play from duels

The Arena uses its own rooms, matchmaking and bout rules. Its queue distinguishes rated competitors from casual, unranked competitors and matches like with like. Rated play can change your Arena rating; casual play is the route when you want an unranked match. Registered accounts are required for rated bouts.

Those distinctions belong to Arena play. The outdoor Challenge interaction is not a shortcut into its rated queue. Read The Arena before joining if rating, eligibility or match rewards matter to your decision.

## Recognize open PvP ground

The Wrothgarian Mountains Open Zone allows attacks without a duel invitation. Its zone law reaches the region's places and dungeons as well as the open wilderness. A doorway is not a promise of safety. Check the zone warning when travelling, and use The Open Zone for the area's wider rules.

The Eltheric Ocean beyond Veilhaven's peace follows the same open-PvP death law. The peace includes the Veil, Veilhaven's surrounding waters and the protected way between them. Beyond it, islands, their towns and their ruins can be dangerous ground. Use The Eltheric Ocean before planning a crossing; a port elsewhere is not automatically another Veilhaven.

## Prepare for an open-zone death

Open-zone death drops eligible possessions from your bag and an accompanying cart into shared remains. Nearby companions' eligible packs also fall under the drop rules. Protected categories include quest or bound possessions and supplies such as potions, ammunition, food and light sources. Letters of credit can drop. The zone drops half the relevant carried gold, rounded down, instead of applying the ordinary death penalty.

Worn gear stays on you after a death to a creature. If another player kills you, the killer may choose one eligible worn piece. That piece has a separate collection process: it is held for the killer, and the final loss depends on collection. Do not read the bag-drop exclusions as blanket protection for everything equipped.

You wait two minutes before returning; pressing Enter does not bypass that hold. Shared remains are lootable by others, so the wait is not private recovery time. For the ordinary rules outside these areas, read Dying online.

## Common mistakes

- Agreeing to spar without checking the ground: open PvP remains dangerous without a challenge.
- Accepting before discussing readiness: agree on space, equipment and when to begin, then follow the countdown.
- Carrying valuables on a practice trip: check your purse, letters, bag, cart and companions before entering an open zone.

## Next

- The Open Zone
- The Eltheric Ocean

understand-the-stakes.excerpt: An ordinary duel is a refereed contest with its own duel vitality. Damage goes to that separate pool. Your real health is never reduced to make the result happen, and the duel does not heal your real character afterward. A duel loss therefore does not send you through the ordinary death-and-respawn penalty.

docs.title: The Open Zone
docs.summary: Understand the Wrothgarian Mountains' shared PvP risk and what can be left behind when you die there.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - The Wrothgarian Mountains are DFO's named Open Zone; treat the trip as PvP-risk travel.
> - A PvP death can leave eligible carried items and cart contents in shared remains.
> - Worn equipment and protected items are excluded by the drop rules.
> - Check your inventory and cart before entering, and collect remains promptly if you die.

## What “open” means

The Wrothgarian Mountains are a shared region where players can fight one another. The Open Zone uses its own death and remains laws, so do not apply ordinary wilderness assumptions to a PvP death.

When a player dies there, the remains service builds a public pile from eligible carried possessions. The law filters protected items and worn gear; eligible bag contents and cart contents can be exposed. Another player may take contents from the remains.

## Reduce what you risk

Before entering, decide what you are willing to carry into a PvP area. Bank valuables and avoid transporting items you cannot afford to lose. If you use a cart, remember it is included in the remains rules; do not assume it shields its contents.

If another player takes only part of a gold pile, the remains service keeps the unclaimed balance available in the shared remains.

## Common mistakes

- Treating the Open Zone like a protected town or ordinary dungeon overlooks its PvP death path.
- Assuming equipment worn at the time of death drops with ordinary bag loot contradicts the protected-worn-gear rule.
- Assuming a remains pile is private or permanent is not supported by the law; another player can interact with eligible contents.

## Next

- The Eltheric Ocean
- Abyss Dungeons

docs.title: The Eltheric Ocean
docs.summary: The open sea past Veilhaven's peace is an online PvP zone with four depth bands and no fixed level gate.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Past Veilhaven's peace, the Eltheric Ocean is an open PvP zone online: other players can fight you, and a death drops your remains.
> - The peace covers Veilhaven, the water around it and the way between it and the Veil; the rest of the sea, its isles, towns and ruins do not.
> - Foes there are about four times an ordinary foe's health and damage, and each deeper band pays more loot: +25%, +50%, +75%, then +100% in the Abyss.
> - A death at sea rises at the nearest freeport's town; a wrecked and boarded ship is not a death but gives up part of its hold.
> - The source sets no universal character-level gate for the crossing; the danger is the sea's law, not a lock on the door.

## Where the peace ends

Online, the sea's shared rules divide it in two. Veilhaven's peace covers the Veil, the water within a short radius of Veilhaven's own pixel where the crossing makes landfall, and the way between them. No player fights within it.

Every other pixel of the sea's box — its isles, their towns and their ruins — runs the same law as the Wrothgarian Mountains' Open Zone: the live flag, fights refereed by the relay, the death's drop and remains, strangers, and foes four times as strong. Offline the sea is the captain's own; the open-PvP rule is online only.

## What waits past it

The deeper you go, the richer and the deadlier. The sea borrows the Open Zone's four rings as depth bands:

| Band | What it is | Loot |
|---|---|---|
| The Shallows | the outer band | +25% |
| The Reaches | the next band | +50% |
| The Deep Aether | the deep band | +75% |
| The Abyss | the heart of the sea | +100% |

Foe health and damage are four times an ordinary foe's in every band; the bands change the loot, not the foe's base strength. A player killed at sea leaves remains, and the death rises at the nearest freeport's town — Veilhaven is one — so a voyage can cost you the trip home as well as the fight. A ship that is wrecked and boarded is a separate case: the captain keeps the hull's hold through death, but the boarder takes a share of the hold as a prize (up to eight of its most valuable pieces, about a third of its worth).

## Reaching the sea

The sea is reached by ship, not by walking or a land carriage. The source does not set a universal character-level requirement for the crossing; it does set the sea's own law once you are past the peace. Use the current map and ship service to establish whether a particular passage is available, and read Owning a ship before you sail into another captain's guns.

Ocean holes can lead to Abyss Dungeon entrances on the seafloor. Treat that as an encounter in the shared sea, not proof that every voyage enters a dungeon; see Abyss Dungeons.

## Common mistakes

- Sailing past the peace without a plan. Other players can attack you there, and a death drops remains; the open sea is not a scenic shortcut.
- Treating the deep bands as only "more loot". The loot rises, but the foes are four times as strong everywhere past the peace.
- Expecting a level gate to protect you. The source sets no universal level requirement, so danger comes from the zone's law and the foes, not from a character-level lock.
- Forgetting the way home. A death rises at the nearest freeport; a wrecked ship is not a death but still costs part of the hold.

## Next

- Owning a ship
- The Open Zone
- Abyss Dungeons

docs.title: Arena seasons and the Royal Tourney
docs.summary: Rated Arena seasons and Crown-city Royal Tourneys have separate schedules, pair limits and entry paths.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - The Herald's Call opens at character level 6 and introduces the Arena.
> - Arena seasons last eight weeks; rated results use a rating ladder.
> - The same pair can count five rated bouts per UTC day and ten per season; later pairings are unrated.
> - The Royal Tourney is a separate seat-week event, with its own sign-up cutoff and pair limit.

## The Arena season

The Arena offers bouts, ratings, exhibitions and private sessions. A season lasts eight weeks from its configured UTC epoch; the Arena week is a seven-day segment used by some reward rules. Do not confuse either clock with the seat week that governs the Royal Tourney.

Rated matchmaking begins within a rating band and widens while it searches. An offer expires if you do not answer within its response window. The rating system starts at 1,000 and uses an Elo calculation; the range enforced by the service is 100 to 4,000.

The same rated pair can have five counted bouts in a UTC day and ten in a season. Further bouts between that same pair remain playable but are no longer rated for the restricted count.

## The Royal Tourney

The Royal Tourney is proclaimed for a seat week rather than an Arena season. The same pair has at most three counted bouts in a UTC day. Its eligibility and schedule depend on the active seat-week proclamation, so check the event notices and registration screen.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming a new Arena season starts at the same time as every player's local week ignores its UTC epoch.
- Treating the per-pair limit as a limit on all of your Arena bouts misstates the scope.
- Carrying the Arena season's eight-week timer over to the Royal Tourney ignores the seat-week event.

## Next

- Elite Gates and the Elite Breach
- Caps, timers and resets

docs.title: Legacy
docs.summary: Project Legacy is an optional family system that carries bounded inheritance and heirlooms across characters.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Project Legacy is a player-owned mod; its family rules are not forced on every online character.
> - A descendant can inherit limited attribute, skill and gold benefits.
> - An eligible worn weapon or armour piece can become a family heirloom and improve across generations.
> - Treat inheritance as optional long-term continuity, not a substitute for a new character's own choices.

## Whether to use Legacy

Project Legacy tracks a family line with births, deaths, heirs and remains. Its enable switch belongs to the player online. If you leave the mod off, the port does not impose its inheritance rules on you.

When enabled, a descendant may receive Blood (attribute gifts) and Hearth (skill gifts), each capped at +3 for an inherited stat or skill. A waiting estate is one quarter of the deceased character's carried gold, up to 9,900 gold. That estate is separate from the death remains, which can contain one tenth of carried gold up to 2,500.

## Heirlooms and blessings

At a final death, the system selects an eligible weapon or armour piece that was worn. An heirloom already in the line remains the chosen piece; otherwise the most valuable eligible worn item is selected. Quest items, summoned items and certain special rarities are excluded.

Each time the lineage carries the heirloom home, it gains one generation, up to five. A weapon gains 5% damage per generation; armour gains 2 armour on the parts it covers per generation. Laying remains to rest can also give a +3 skill blessing, with a +9 cap on any one skill across the family.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming Legacy is an online rule for everyone ignores its player-owned enable state.
- Confusing the inherited estate with gold in remains combines two separate portions of carried gold.
- Expecting every equipped item to become an heirloom ignores the eligibility filter and the single selected keepsake.

## Next

- Choices that are hard to undo
- Caps, timers and resets

docs.title: Endgame goals
docs.summary: Choose a long-term goal, understand its demands, and decide what finishing means for your character.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Choose a goal you want to play toward; the systems do not share one finish line.
> - Renown stops at 50, while selected mastered skills can reach 200.
> - Questline levels introduce activities; they are not universal admission levels for every related encounter.
> - Arena seasons last eight weeks. Other goals use different clocks.

## Decide what finished means

You can finish a story, settle on a character build, complete a demanding encounter, compete for a season or continue a family line. You can choose any of these stopping points.

The original Daggerfall main quest remains part of your character's story. Online play does not replace it with a compulsory shared campaign. Your quest state stays yours, even when you share quest foes with a party. The added introduction and endgame questlines lead you into online systems; they do not make the original main quest a prerequisite for parties, guilds, Renown or shared events.



## Choose your long-term goal

| Goal | Gate | What it asks | What it gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reach Renown 50 and shape the Firmament | Online progression; Written in the Stars opens at character level 3 | Earn capped Renown XP and plan star spending | Online growth and a chosen set of Firmament benefits |
| Master selected skills and choose paths | A class skill at 100 and a free mastery slot; paths require a mastered pair | Sustained, relevant skill use and permanent mastery choices | Progress toward 200, milestone benefits and eligible specialisation effects |
| Complete the Elite Breach chain | Burning Doors opens at level 10, registered online; Covens' Hoard then Weir Road | Follow witnessed deeds, obtain a Weir Key and take Redoubts | Questline honours and the encounter's rewards |
| Defeat an Abyss Dungeon | Shared event available; its introduction opens at level 12, registered online | Find the active entrance and complete the shared challenge | Encounter spoils and the relevant witnessed questline deed |
| Hold a city seat | Registered player-guild participation; founding has separate requirements | Coordinate influence and contend for control across seat weeks | A guild seat and its governing choices |
| Compete in Arena or a Royal Tourney | Arena introduction at level 6 online; Tourney follows its proclamation | Repeated refereed bouts against other players | Rated standings, seasonal competition or Tourney results |
| Continue a Legacy | Enable Project Legacy and establish a family | Plan succession and recover eligible family heirlooms | Bounded inheritance and continuity across characters |
| Explore the Eltheric Ocean | Reach it by ship; no universal character-level gate | Manage a voyage, dangerous foes and open PvP beyond the peace | Exploration and depth-band loot opportunities |

## Renown and the Firmament

Renown is separate from your character level. Reaching its cap is a bounded growth goal, not proof that your quests, skills or equipment are complete. The Firmament turns that progress into choices: you earn 2 stars per Renown after the first and spend them along its available branches.

Review the Firmament before spending. An hourly account cap limits Renown earning across characters, so changing characters does not create another full allowance for that hour.

## Masteries and specialisation paths

Master Skills is active online. At 100, you must choose an eligible class skill for mastery before it can pass the normal cap. Your slots allow two primary skills, two major skills and one minor skill. Mastery choices are permanent; selecting a specialisation and selecting a mastery are different decisions.

Mastered skills can reach 200, but their later points cost more uses and contribute reduced effective value. The use-cost multipliers rise through four, eight and sixteen times the ordinary requirement. Challenging foes and relevant activity matter; repeating weak actions is not a reliable route to mastery.

A mastered pair of spell schools can open an arcane path, while a mastered pair of weapon skills can open a martial path. You can hold one of each family. Compare each path with how you play. A path reset does not refund the mastery slots that made the path possible. Read masteries and specialisations before committing those slots.

## Encounters, control and seasons

Elite Breach and Abyss goals depend on more than your damage output. Questline credit can require a service-witnessed deed in order, and a shared dungeon must be in an admitting phase. The level that opens an introduction letter does not guarantee that a particular event is available when you arrive.

City control asks for coordination across a seat week. Arena uses an eight-week season from its configured UTC epoch; Royal Tourney follows a separate seat-week proclamation. A Tourney notice does not announce a fresh Arena season.

Legacy and the sea support less fixed endpoints. Legacy carries limited gifts and an eligible heirloom through a family; it is an optional player-owned system online. The sea offers voyages rather than a universal completion bar. Beyond Veilhaven's peace, open PvP and death drops make preparation part of the goal.

## How much time to allow

The source sets event windows, caps, cooldowns and season lengths. It does not set one playtime estimate for finishing DFO or reaching every cap. Nor does an eight-week season require you to play every day. Your target, party availability and setbacks affect the time involved.

Use caps and timers to plan around the activity you choose. Shared encounters may require a suitable event window.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a questline's opening level as the admission rule for every encounter it introduces.
- Spending permanent mastery slots before checking a desired path's pair.
- Assuming all endgame activities reset with the Arena season.

## Next

- Elite Gates and the Elite Breach
- Arena seasons and the Royal Tourney

docs.title: How this guide is checked
docs.summary: What the page footer means, what a Draft badge means, and how to report a mistake.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Every page names the game commit it was checked against in its footer.
> - Numbers that come from the game's source are re-read automatically; other numbers are checked by hand.
> - A Draft badge means the page has been checked against the source, but not yet read end to end by the maintainer.
> - If a rule looks wrong, tell us where — the Discord is the quickest route.

## Two kinds of checking

The Handbook is not copied from another wiki. Each page is written against DFO's own source and design records.

- Rules. A writer reads the code paths that actually run online, then names the file and symbol in the page's
  Sources disclosure. Combat, loot, travel and the online lane are the usual places where the online rule differs from
  classic Daggerfall.
- Numbers. Values in the fact registry are read straight from the source when the guide syncs, so those update when
  the game changes. A number typed by hand is only as current as the page's checked-against commit.

The footer tells you both: the game commit the numbers were read at, and the older commit the page was last reviewed at.
If those are far apart, read the page with that in mind.

## What the badges mean

- Draft — the page has been checked against the game's source, but no one has yet read it end to end for sense,
  completeness or contradictions with other pages. Treat its rules as sourced but its coverage as unfinished.
- No badge — the page has been through that read-through and is the most reliable state the guide has.
- Planned — the page is announced in the structure but not written yet.

A Draft page is not a guess. It is a page whose claims are cited but whose practical advice may still be thin.

## What we do not do

- We do not publish live player data, seat holders, prices or anything read through a signed-in session.
- We do not include Daggerfall's game assets, extracted art, sounds or copied book text.
- We do not claim a rule the source does not set; where the source is silent, the page says so.

## If a page is wrong

Tell us what the page says, what the game does, and how you know. The
DFO Discord is the quickest route to the maintainer; the project's
issue tracker is for game bugs rather than Handbook
corrections. A wrong rule matters more than a typo: include the commit in the footer and, if you can, the file or
symbol that disagrees.

## Next

- The glossary
- What changed

docs.title: Glossary
docs.summary: Short definitions for the game's world, controls, online systems, events, currencies and progression terms used in the handbook, grouped A–Z.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Entries are grouped A–Z; the first use of a term on any page shows its definition on hover.
> - Each entry defines a term as DFO Online uses it.
> - Some familiar terms name DFO's own systems or the mods it forces on, not classic Daggerfall's rules.
> - A term that is missing or wrong can be reported; How this guide is checked says where.

## A–C

### Abyss Dungeon
The player-facing name for the shared, timed dungeon whose internal system name is Super Dungeon.

### Abyss phase
One of the shared dungeon's states as it rises, is found, falls or disappears.

### Account
The service identity that owns account-wide balances, event receipts and limits.

### Arena
The online system for rated bouts, exhibitions and private sessions.

### Arena rating
The numerical score the Arena updates from rated outcomes.

### Arena season
An eight-week rating and reward period measured from a UTC epoch.

### Arena week
A seven-day segment used by Arena-related event reward rules.

### Attribute
One of a character's core numerical traits used by advancement and combat systems.

### Bank of the Empire
The online service that exchanges Marks for gold.

### Bounty
A hunt taken from a town's Bounty Board and held by a character for one game day.

### Carried remains
Eligible bag or cart contents left behind by a player's Open Zone death.

### Census
The account count used when the Abyss Dungeon director selects an eligible region.

### Champion
A named enemy promotion with a visible champion trait.

### Character level
The skill-driven character progression level, distinct from Renown.

### Chat channel
A recipient group chosen from chat tabs or a channel command.

### Clock hour
The fixed hour bucket, reset on the hour, used for the Renown hourly limit and the services' request limits.

### Combat Marks
Marks earned from Dagon's Breach, town raids, the sea serpent, Redoubts and Starfall, under one shared account ceiling per UTC day.

### Court writ
A profession delivery that grants Marks and profession progression under an account limit.

### Craft
A profession track that can advance through crafting actions.

## D–F

### Daggerfall
The 1996 role-playing game The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall, of which DFO Online is an independent reimplementation. DFO needs your own copy of Daggerfall's original game data (ARENA2) to run; see What DFO Online is.

### Daggerfall Unity
The open-source Daggerfall reimplementation (MIT, by Interkarma and contributors) that DFO Online began as a port of. DFO keeps it as the reference for its data and logic, not a target to match, so offline Daggerfall Unity rules can differ from online play; see Which rules apply online.

### Dagon's Breach
A scheduled gate event with account-scoped reward claims.

### Deep Delver
A Mining specialisation: dungeon veins yield double, and every vein in the dungeon is marked on the compass.

### Default binding
The key or button assigned to an action when no saved rebind overrides it.

### DFO Online
The browser-played, online reimplementation of Daggerfall at daggerfalljs.dev, with shared-world systems and rules on top of the Daggerfall Unity-derived port. See What DFO Online is.

### Dice roll
A chat command that rolls a parsed dice expression.

### Elite
A promoted foe enabled for a character's own world after the elite gate is met.

### Elite Breach
The shared Elite Gates event whose halls are called Redoubts.

### Elite Dungeon
A dungeon instance with elite foes and its own respawn timing.

### Elite foe
An enemy with the elite promotion and its associated enhanced stats or rewards.

### Elite Gate
A gate in the Weir Road and Elite Breach progression.

### Emote
A chat-triggered gesture such as waving or bowing.

### Enhanced AI
The port's enemy-behaviour enhancement, forced on for everyone online. It supplies the telegraphed attacks that land when their wind-up completes; see Fighting.

### Event receipt
An account-service record used to prevent duplicate claims for a reward event.

### Fighters Guild
One of DFO's four NPC guilds, offering combat training and guild services at its halls; you apply there like any NPC guild. See The NPC guilds.

### Firmament
The online star tree with two point pools: Stars from Renown, which buy any star, and Craft points from profession ranks, which buy life-ring stars only.

## G–I

### Game day
A day of the shared event clock, two real hours long, used by scheduled events such as Dagon's Breach and town raids. It is not the sky's day you see in the world.

### Gold
The character's own carried and saved currency, separate from Marks. It has weight, is exposed to the death penalty, and the Bank of the Empire exchanges Marks for gold one way; see Money and markets.

### Gothway Garden
The first town out of Privateer's Hold and the setting of the handbook's first-town pages; see Leaving the Hold.

### Guild
A player organization with its own treasury and city-seat activity.

### Guild channel
Chat addressed to members of the player's guild.

### Guild Marks
Marks held in a player guild's shared treasury.

### Heir
A later member of a Project Legacy family line who can receive bounded inheritance.

### Heirloom
An eligible weapon or armour piece carried across Project Legacy generations.

### Hour That Was Not
The questline, opening at character level 12, that introduces Abyss Dungeon content.

### Iliac Bay
The region of Tamriel covered by Daggerfall's world map, and the name the handbook uses for DFO's shared game world. Its regions, settlements, wilderness and dungeons are the places you travel between; see Danger and regions.

## J–L

### Knightly order
A chivalric NPC organization (one of the realm's ten knightly orders). All orders share one membership slot and offer training and services; see The NPC guilds.

### Language channel
An optional chat channel selected with the language command.

### LFG channel
An opt-in channel for looking for a group.

### Local chat
Nearby in-character speech between players in range.

## M–O

### Mages Guild
One of DFO's four NPC guilds, offering magic services, training and rank-gated teleport at its halls. See The NPC guilds and Mages Guild services.

### Market listing
A timed item offer occupying one of an account's active listing slots.

### Market order
A timed buy request occupying one of an account's active order slots.

### Marks
The online currency used by account and guild services.

### Mentor mode
The automatic scaling that plays a higher-level party member at about the party's level when the party is well below theirs.

### Motherlode
A scheduled shared resource event with a limited number of world appearances.

### NPC guild
A town-based organization — a Fighters Guild, Mages Guild, temple or knightly order — that you apply to at its hall for rank, training and services. It is not a player guild; see Guild and The NPC guilds.

### Open Zone
The Wrothgarian Mountains region where PvP deaths can leave shared remains.

## P–R

### Pair limit
A counted-bout limit applied to a particular opponent pair rather than all of one player's matches.

### Party
A player group with shared activity rules and leader travel tools.

### Physical Combat and Armor Overhaul (PCAAO)
The balance mod that DFO forces on and locks at its shipped defaults online. Online hit chance, damage, armour, shield blocks and racial weapon bonuses come from it; see Which rules apply online.

### Privateer's Hold
The starting dungeon where a new character begins. Online its public room can be entered once per character, and leaving it leads toward Gothway Garden; see Your first minutes.

### Profession request window
The clock hour within which an account's requests to the profession service are counted.

### Project Legacy
The player-owned mod that tracks family lines, heirs and heirlooms.

### Redoubt
A named encounter inside the Elite Breach.

### Redoubt receipt
An account record that marks a weekly reward claim for one Redoubt.

### Region channel
Chat addressed to players in the current region.

### Renown
Online progression earned from play and tracked separately from character level.

### Renown track
One character's progress along the Renown ladder.

### Roleplay & Realism
The balance mod that DFO forces on at its shipped defaults online. It supplies the online encumbrance rules (weight slows you past 75% of your limit), the loan limits and the repair rules; see Which rules apply online.

### Royal Tourney
A duel ladder held through a proclaimed seat week in a crown city, with its own counted-bout limit.

## S–U

### Shared action key
A key assigned to more than one action, with behavior determined by the active context.

### Soul Cake
A collectible found during the Witches' Festival under account limits.

### Starfall
A Witches' Festival event in which fallen stars must be held against waves of foes; a star held pays Renown and Marks, under the combat Marks ceiling.

### Super Dungeon
The internal code name for the player-facing Abyss Dungeon.

### Temple
A religious NPC organization (one of the eight divines' temples). All temples share one membership slot and offer healing, training and penance services; see The NPC guilds.

### Tide
A condition rolled each seat week for each kingdom, the Marches and the Free Lands; depending on the Tide it changes gathering or fishing yields, influence, festival costs, couriers or sea travel.

### Trade channel
An opt-in chat channel for trade conversations.

### Unleveled Loot
The balance mod that DFO forces on online; an item's material comes from luck, place and source rather than your character level. See Loot rarity.

### Unstuck
A command flow that moves a stranded character to a permitted recovery point.

### UTC day
The midnight-to-midnight UTC period used by many account daily limits.

## V–Z

### Weir Key
A stackable inventory item used by the Elite Gates progression.

### The Weir Road
The questline that leads into Elite Gate progression.

### Wild remains
The shared drop record left after a death in the Open Zone.

### Witches' Festival
A seasonal event with Soul Cakes and Starfall activity.

### World channel
Chat addressed across the online world.

## Action names

These entries are input actions, not game systems. Keys and commands lists their default bindings and how to rebind them.

### ActChoice
The action that chooses what Interact starts at a gathering spot, such as gathering herbs or foraging food at an herb patch.

### BoatSailUp
The Come Sail Away action that sets more sail at a ship's helm.

### FreeMouse
The action that releases or recaptures the pointer for interface use.

### LegacyFamily
The Project Legacy action that opens the family view.

### ModeWheel
The held action that opens the interaction-mode wheel: Steal, Grab, Info or Talk.

### Quick Loot All
The action that takes the loot currently offered by a container or source.

### Quick Loot Open
The action that opens the highlighted loot container.

### QuickDial
The action that opens the four-way dial to your skills, items, map and magic.

### SocialInteract
The action that opens the social menu on another player, or the friends and party panel when nobody is in reach.

### WeaponTechnique
The dedicated input action for using a weapon's technique line.

docs.title: Which rules apply online
docs.summary: DFO Online folds in many mods; this page shows which are forced on for everyone, which are locked at their defaults, and which are yours to switch.
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - DFO Online is Daggerfall Unity plus many mods, some built into the game and some you can toggle.
> - Online, every mod falls into one of three groups: forced on for the shared world, balance mods locked at
>   their defaults, or yours to switch (looks and sound only).
> - Combat, loot, enemies, travel, encumbrance, loans and repairs follow the locked mods' rules, not classic
>   Daggerfall's. Advice written for single-player Daggerfall or Daggerfall Unity is often wrong online.
> - Every rule in this handbook is checked against the version that actually runs online.

## Why this matters

Many of the game's formulas exist more than once in its code: the classic version, and a mod's replacement. Offline,
your mod switches decide which one runs. Online, DFO decides for everyone, so that two players in the same dungeon
fight by the same rules, see the same towns and roll loot from the same tables.

If you read a guide for classic Daggerfall or for Daggerfall Unity, check its numbers against this handbook. Hit
chances, damage, racial bonuses, loot materials, encumbrance and loan limits all differ online.

## The three groups

| Group | What it means | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Forced on for the shared world | Switched on for every player, because the world must be the same for everyone: the ground, the towns, the sea, the raids | Basic Roads, World of Daggerfall, Beautiful Cities and Villages, Detailed Ships, World Events: Raiding Parties, Travel Options, Immersive Travel, Iliac Puddle No More |
| Balance mods, locked whole | Forced on, and every one of their settings held at its shipped default; you can't change their dials online | Physical Combat and Armor Overhaul, Meaner Monsters, Daggerfall Enemy Expansion, Unleveled Loot, Roleplay & Realism and its Items add-on |
| Yours to switch | Change only what your own screen shows or your speakers play; they never change a rule | Dynamic Skies, Seasons, Weapon Widget, Eye of the Beholder, Immersive Footsteps, ambience, foliage and weather effects |

The game's own enhancements follow the same idea: those that shape the shared world (Enhanced AI, Loot rarity,
weather, landforms, questlines, naval encounters) are on for everyone; visual quality settings are yours.

## Every mod and feature

This table is generated from the game's own online settings ledger each time the handbook is built, so it is always
current:

table online.ruleset


## What the locked mods change

| System | The rule online | Not the rule online |
|---|---|---|
| Hitting and damage | Physical Combat and Armor Overhaul: your Agility, Speed and Luck against the target's; hit chance always 3% to 97%; racial weapon bonuses; attribute-based Expertise | Classic Daggerfall's hit and damage formulas |
| Enemy attacks | Enhanced AI: telegraphed attacks land when their wind-up completes; ordinary swings still follow the attack timer | Classic timing alone |
| Enemies | Meaner Monsters and Daggerfall Enemy Expansion: tougher foes and a wider roster, decided by the dungeon's host for everyone | The base enemy tables |
| Loot | Unleveled Loot and Loot rarity: materials come from luck, place and source, not your level; a shared container's contents are rolled by the shared rules | Classic level-scaled loot |
| Carrying | Roleplay & Realism: carrying more than 75% of your limit slows you and drains fatigue | Classic "no penalty until the limit" |
| Loans | Roleplay & Realism's loan table, divided by ten for the Empire's bank: 1,000 gold per level | Offline loan limits |
| Repairs and selling | Roleplay & Realism Items: an item's condition affects its sale price; magic items can always be repaired | Classic repair and price rules |
| Travel | Travel Options: journeys over land are walked or ridden in real time; the carriage driver is the paid land shortcut | Daggerfall's instant map travel |

## Settings that stay yours

A few rules still depend on a choice you make online. Pages that depend on one say so.

| Setting | Default | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| Climates & Calories | Boons | How hunger, thirst and temperature affect you (Off, Boons, Casual or Hard) |
| Horse care and wagon upkeep | Boons | How much feeding and wear matter |
| Levelling style | Classic | Fixed at character creation; online characters use classic levelling |
| Shield Widget | on | How your own shield blocks are shown and resolved for you as the defender |

docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - DFO keeps Daggerfall's world, data and many of its systems, but online it replaces the rules that decide combat, enemies, loot, travel, death and progression.
> - Your classic or Daggerfall Unity instincts are usually right about what exists and often wrong about what it costs or how it resolves.
> - Read this page before following an old guide. Then use Which rules apply online as the index to every replacement.
> - Offline DFO does keep classic rules; these changes describe online play unless a line says otherwise.

## The short version

Online, DFO is not Daggerfall with players in it. It is a rebuilt game that uses Daggerfall's data and presentation, with a fixed online ruleset on top. The world map, dungeons, quests, items and lore are largely the ones you know. The maths that decides whether you hit, what drops, how you travel, what death costs and how you grow has been replaced or locked.

The working rule for a veteran: assume a familiar rule has a replacement until you have checked it. The rest of this page lists the replacements a player notices first.

## 1. Overland travel is travelled, not teleported

Classic Daggerfall's map travel is instant. Online, a trip over land is a walked or ridden journey in real time, and the carriage driver is the paid shortcut; ships sail only from ports (src/systems/online/onlineLane.js: ONLINEROOMMODKEYS forces Travel Options and Immersive Travel; see Which rules apply online, "Travel"). Party travel is the one fast trip: a follower can pay a fare to reach the leader without advancing world time.

## 2. Hit chance and damage are PCAAO's

Online combat runs Physical Combat and Armor Overhaul, not the classic formulas. Your Agility, Speed and Luck meet the target's; hit chance is clamped to 3%–97%; racial weapon bonuses and attribute-based Expertise apply (src/combat/pcaao.js; online-ruleset.md, "Hitting and damage"). A hit that a classic guide calls certain can miss here, and a build that relied on a classic to-hit shortcut does not work the same way.

## 3. Enemies telegraph their blows

Enhanced AI is on online. An enemy's heavy attack lands when its wind-up completes, and the tell is your chance to move, block or interrupt (src/characters/enemy/enemyAttack.js: telegraphed blows; online-ruleset.md, "Enemy attacks"). Standing in front of a wind-up and trading blows is a classic habit that now costs health.

## 4. The enemy roster and its scaling are not classic

Meaner Monsters and Daggerfall Enemy Expansion are forced on, and the place you are in sets the threat more than your level does (src/systems/online/onlineLane.js: both mods locked whole; src/systems/skillSoftcap.js: place threat and foe scaling). A low-level character can meet a foe a classic guide would never place there, and a high-level character does not automatically outscale an easy dungeon.

## 5. Loot is unleveled

Unleveled Loot and Loot rarity are on. Materials and rarity come from luck, place and source rather than your character level (src/systems/unleveledLoot.js, src/systems/loot/lootRarity.js; online-ruleset.md, "Loot"). The old "level up and the loot improves" loop does not hold. Better places drop better things, and a shared container's contents are rolled under the shared rules.

## 6. Carrying, loans and repairs follow Roleplay & Realism

Encumbrance slows and drains fatigue once you pass 75% of your carry limit; loans use Roleplay & Realism's table divided by ten for the Empire's bank; an item's condition affects its sale price, and magic items can always be repaired (src/systems/roleplayRealism/rrRealism.js; src/systems/banking.js: EMPIRELOANDIVISOR; online-ruleset.md, "Carrying", "Loans", "Repairs and selling"). The classic "no penalty until the limit" and the old loan sizes are gone online.

## 7. Death is not a reload

Offline, death ends the run and you load a save. Online, you respawn after a countdown at a safe place, at reduced health, and lose part of the gold you carry; banked gold is safe (src/ui/deathScreen.js: DEATH4; src/systems/deathPenalty.js; docs/23-playing-online.md: a tenth of carried gold). Do not plan an online fight around reloading to undo it.

## 8. You cannot load mid-session online

Online, loading a save during play is disabled, including quick load (src/scenes/dungeonContext.js: ONLINE-LOAD1). The game checkpoints your character as you go and on exit (src/scenes/world.js: online checkpoints and exit autosave). The classic habit of saving before a decision and reloading after a bad outcome has no online equivalent.

## 9. Mods are not yours to choose

DFO has no mod support: you cannot install DFU mods or Nexus mods, and there is no load order to manage (https://daggerfalljs.dev/, "Not finished"). The game ships a fixed set of mods and settings; online, the shared and balance ones are forced, and only looks-and-sound switches remain yours (src/systems/online/onlineLane.js; online-ruleset.md). A "best mods" list is advice for another game.

## 10. Your settings are Features rows, not a mod list

The switches you do control are the game's own Features entries, and online several are still your choice: Climates & Calories, horse care, wagon upkeep and similar personal systems. A few matter a lot: survival defaults to Boons, which takes nothing from you and rewards needs met, rather than the harsher tiers a mod veteran may remember (src/systems/features.js; src/systems/survival/difficulty.js: SURVIVALDEFAULT).

## 11. Marks are not gold

Online adds a second currency, Marks, held by your account rather than your character. They are earned from witnessed activity and spent on the market, guild seats and other account systems. The Bank of the Empire exchanges them for gold one way, at 8 gold per Mark, up to 300 Marks per UTC day, and the record values a Mark at about 10 gold of play (src/net/marksLaw.js: MARKSBANK, MARKWORTHGOLD). Gold remains the character's currency; do not treat the two as interchangeable.

## 12. Renown is a second ladder

Online, character level is only one progression. Renown runs 1–50, comes from kills, quests and events, and pays for the Firmament's stars; the Firmament's passive tree is online-only and sleeps offline (src/net/renown.js; src/systems/firmamentLive.js). A classic veteran who ignores Renown falls behind on the passive bonuses that online characters assume.

## 13. Guilds promote at once, and stop at 7

Online, an earned guild promotion is applied when you next open the services, without the classic wait; the 28-day review delay is not used for earned promotions (src/systems/guild/guilds.js: updateRank, the PROMO-NOW rule; docs/23-playing-online.md). Personal online rank stops at 7; 8 and 9 are chapter seats. Training is also its own law online: a member pays 100 × character level a session, a non-member 400 × level, sessions are capped at skill 50, and a character can train once per 12 game hours (src/systems/guild/guildServiceActions.js: TRAININGCOOLDOWNMINUTES; guildServices.js: trainingPrice).

## 14. Quests behave like an online game's

Quest failure costs no faction standing online, unlike classic Daggerfall's reputation loss (src/systems/quest/quest.js: failureFree). Quest deadlines charge only played time, while waits and delays are cut to a short online wait (src/systems/quest/clock.js). DFO adds questlines with level, account and event gates (src/systems/questlines/qlLines.js), and a quest's dungeon can be taken as a private instance for you and your party (docs/23-playing-online.md, "Dungeons without the crowds"). The old advice to save before a quest and reload if it goes wrong belongs to offline play.

## 15. Other players change the world around you

Online is one shared world: other players fight in the same dungeons, public dungeon kills and containers are shared, and a cleared public dungeon respawns on a real-time clock. Mentor mode switches on automatically when a party's reference level is well below yours, scaling you down without taking your real progress (src/systems/mentorMode.js; docs/23-playing-online.md, "Group up"). This is not in any classic guide because classic Daggerfall had no other players.

## What did not change

The map and regions, the dungeons' data, the quests' scripts, the items, the races and classes, the guilds' identities and most of the lore are the Daggerfall you know. Character creation still asks the classic questions; the difference is which rules those choices meet after you enter the world.

## Common mistakes

- Following a classic walkthrough's numbers. Hit chances, loot, travel times and death costs are the online rules now.
- Saving to undo an online mistake. Mid-session loading is disabled online.
- Looking for a mod list. DFO does not accept mods.
- Ignoring Renown and the Firmament. They are part of online power, not optional cosmetics.
- Expecting a guild promotion wait. Earned promotions apply when you next open services.

## Next

- Which rules apply online
- Offline and online

docs.title: Caps, timers and resets
docs.summary: The limits players meet use different scopes: account totals, hourly service windows, event clocks, pair counts and world respawns.
headings: World timers are not personal caps
docs.body:
> [!tip] At a glance
> - Check whether a limit is per character, account, event, pair or service before planning around it.
> - Daily account limits generally use the UTC day; the hourly service limits reset on the clock hour, not at midnight.
> - World schedules and dungeon respawns are clocks, not personal earning caps.
> - Event dates can change; use the live event notice for the current calendar.

## Account and service limits

These are the limits most likely to affect repeated activity. A request-rate limit controls how often the service accepts operations; it does not necessarily cap how much you can gather or earn. Every hourly limit below counts within a fixed clock hour and starts again at the top of the next one.

| Activity | Limit or clock | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Renown | 15000 XP per account per clock hour, across all its characters; at most 5,000 XP counted per report (the game reports about once a minute) | Account; Court writ Renown is credited on a separate path. |
| Profession service | 600 requests per clock hour (a harvest, a withdrawal, a delivery or a choice each count) | Account operation-rate limit, not a daily harvest counter. |
| Marks service | 120 operations per clock hour (an exchange or a guild move each count) | Account operation-rate limit. |
| Combat Marks | 150 Marks per UTC day from Dagon's Breach, town raids, the sea serpent, Redoubts and Starfall together | Shared account UTC-day ceiling across combat reward sources. |
| Bank of the Empire | 300 Marks exchanged for gold per day (never gold for Marks), at 8 gold per Mark | Account UTC day. |
| Marks balance | 10,000,000 | Account or guild balance ceiling. |
| Market | 30 active listings and 20 active orders; 60 new posts and 120 other operations per clock hour | Account; listings last 72 hours, orders last seven days. |
| Gathering nodes | A node slot resets at 00:00 UTC and is once per character per day | Character and node slot; there is no general daily harvest counter, though rare high-tier hides are limited to three a day. |
| Court writs | 3 writs | Account per UTC day. |
| Motherlodes | Three world lodes each UTC day, at most 20 strikers per lode; one Marks reward per account per day | Shared world schedule plus account receipt. |
| Festival Soul Cakes | 120 finds per account per UTC day; 1,500 find requests per day | Account; event dates are configuration and can change. |
| Starfall | Up to nine stars counted per account per UTC day (the day the star fell) | Account; its Marks also count toward the combat Marks ceiling. |
| Bounties | Four postings per town board per game day; four active bounties per character | Game-day board schedule; a taken bounty lapses after one game day. |

## Event clocks and pair limits

| Event | Clock or limit | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Dagon's Breach | One gate per game day of the event clock (two real hours); entry window is 20:00–22:00 on that clock, about ten real minutes | Scheduled world event; a registered account claims each gate at most once. |
| Town raids | Same two-real-hour game-day schedule; at most 32 raids per game day | One receipt per account per raid; the source establishes no separate daily raid count. |
| Sea serpent | Rises every second event-clock day (every four real hours) at the dawn watch | One account receipt per serpent. |
| Arena | Eight-week season; same rated pair counts five bouts per UTC day and ten per season | Later bouts between that pair can be played unrated. |
| Royal Tourney | Same pair counts three bouts per UTC day | Seat-week tournament, open through the week it is proclaimed; separate from the Arena season. |
| Seat influence | 60 Watch per account per UTC day; gate influence at most 900 and Renown influence at most 400 per account per week; 2,000 per account per seat per week from all sources | Seat week; the Turning occurs Sunday at 18:00 UTC. |
| Abyss Dungeon | 48-hour unbeaten lifespan; three-minute collapse after defeat; two-hour cooldown; census needs two accounts | Shared world event, not a personal entry cooldown. |

## World timers are not personal caps

Ordinary dungeon foes and containers respawn 20 minutes after they fell or were emptied, Elite Dungeon ones after 40 minutes, and those in an Abyss Dungeon or the Open Zone's halls after 30 minutes. Each foe and container keeps its own clock, whoever comes and goes. These govern respawns in a world, not how many times your account may earn a reward. The Abyss Dungeon's own rise and fall follow its shared event cycle, above.

Online account daily caps use UTC boundaries, while service-rate limits use clock-hour windows. Each daily book turns its UTC day at its own moment — up to ten minutes after midnight — so a cap or node slot can lag a little past 00:00 UTC; see src/net/dayTurn.js DAYTURNSPREADMS. Event schedules run on the shared event clock (a game day every two real hours), which is not the sky's hour you see in the world. A seasonal event's active dates are configurable. When the event notice and an old calendar disagree, follow the current notice.

## A daily and weekly checklist

Keep this page open while you play. The boxes are saved in this browser and reset on the game's UTC clock; the limits themselves are in the tables above.

checklist daily
- [ ] Check the Notice Board's Seat and Work tabs for writs and bounties you can fill.
- [ ] Spend the day's combat Marks and bank exchange before they reset.
- [ ] Clear the day's gathering node slots before the day turns.
- [ ] Post or refresh market listings you want seen today.
- [ ] Check the HUD event board for today's shared events.


checklist weekly
- [ ] Check the guild's seat pledge before the Friday 18:00 UTC lock.
- [ ] Check the seat standings before the Sunday 18:00 UTC Turning.
- [ ] Review Arena and Royal Tourney pair counts before a rated bout.
- [ ] Review your Renown and craft plans before spending stars or a craft rank.


## Common mistakes

- Treating an operation-rate limit as a daily reward cap can make you stop an activity for the wrong reason.
- Treating all daily resets as local midnight ignores the UTC account bucket.
- Counting an event schedule as a personal cooldown mixes shared world timing with account receipts.
- Treating the Arena pair limit as a cap on every match ignores its pair scope.

## Next

- Arena seasons and the Royal Tourney
- Questions new players ask
